title: Entangling power of neural networks
summary: Characterizing the complexity of correlations between subsystems is a fundamental task across information theory, machine learning, and science. In quantum physics, neural networks have found increasing application in learning wavefunctions. Here we introduce the entangling power of an encoder-decoder neural network, which quantifies its ability to generate entanglement between subsystems, dependent on a latent space dimension $K$ and the complexity class of the decoder. We exactly calculate this quantity for polynomial decoders of degree $p$ acting on a $K$-dimensional latent space. Our results establish the exponential entangling power of neural networks with modest resources. More broadly, our work provides a framework for analyzing correlations in machine learning that generalizes the notion of the Schmidt rank in entanglement theory.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces and exactly computes the "entangling power" of encoder-decoder neural networks—a quantity measuring how much entanglement a neural network can generate between subsystems—as a function of latent space dimension K and decoder complexity class. The authors prove exponential entangling power for polynomial decoders and generalize the Schmidt rank notion to machine learning correlation analysis.
AI.motivation: Characterizing correlations between subsystems is fundamental across information theory, machine learning, and science, yet quantum entanglement generation by neural networks has not been systematically quantified. The authors aim to provide a rigorous framework for analyzing how neural networks generate entanglement, bridging quantum physics and machine learning.
AI.method: The authors define the entangling power of an encoder-decoder neural network based on its latent space dimension K and the complexity class (degree p) of the decoder. They derive exact formulas for this quantity specifically for polynomial decoders acting on a K-dimensional latent space.
AI.result: Exact calculations show that neural networks with polynomial decoders possess exponential entangling power even with modest resources (small K and low degree p). This demonstrates that relatively simple neural architectures can generate exponentially large amounts of entanglement.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes a rigorous connection between neural network complexity and quantum entanglement generation, providing a new framework that generalizes the Schmidt rank from entanglement theory to characterize correlations in machine learning models more broadly.

title: Local Uniqueness of the Born Rule on Categories with Complex-Weighted Morphisms
summary: I prove a local uniqueness theorem for the Born rule in the setting of small categories equipped with complex morphism weights and path-amplitude probability functionals. Given (i) non-negativity, (ii) polynomiality of bounded total degree, (iii) global U(1) invariance, (iv) classical-limit additivity over mutually exclusive paths, and (v) normalization, I show that the probability assignment P: C -> R>=0 is uniquely determined to be P(z) = |z|^2. The notion of mutually exclusive paths is given a precise categorical formulation as the absence of a shared factorization through any common morphism. I relate the result to reconstructions of quantum probability due to Gleason, Hardy, and Chiribella-D'Ariano-Perinotti, and identify the extension to global coherence under morphism composition as an open problem connected to synthetic probability theory in Markov categories. The Born rule emerges as the unique locally consistent probability law on complex amplitudes, fixed solely by phase invariance and classical-limit behavior, independent of any Hilbert-space framework.

AI.tldr: This paper proves a local uniqueness theorem for the Born rule within small categories with complex morphism weights and path-amplitude probability functionals. Under five conditions (non-negativity, polynomiality of bounded total degree, global U(1) invariance, classical-limit additivity over mutually exclusive paths, and normalization), the probability assignment is uniquely determined to be P(z) = |z|². The notion of mutually exclusive paths is formalized categorically as the absence of shared factorization through a common morphism, and the result is related to reconstructions by Gleason, Hardy, and Chiribella-D'Ariano-Perinotti.
AI.motivation: The paper aims to derive the Born rule as the unique locally consistent probability law on complex amplitudes without presupposing any Hilbert-space framework, providing a purely categorical and combinatorial foundation for quantum probability.
AI.method: The author works in the setting of small categories with complex morphism weights and path-amplitude probability functionals. The proof relies on five axiomatic conditions: non-negativity, polynomiality of bounded total degree, global U(1) invariance, classical-limit additivity over mutually exclusive paths (defined categorically as the absence of shared factorization through any common morphism), and normalization. These constraints jointly force the unique form P(z) = |z|².
AI.result: The probability assignment is uniquely determined to be P(z) = |z|² under the stated axioms. The result is related to well-known reconstructions of quantum probability (Gleason, Hardy, and Chiribella-D'Ariano-Perinotti), and the Born rule emerges as the unique locally consistent law on complex amplitudes determined solely by phase invariance and classical-limit additivity.
AI.conclusion: The Born rule follows uniquely from phase invariance and classical-limit behavior in a categorical setting independent of Hilbert-space structure. The extension to global coherence under morphism composition is identified as an open problem, connected to synthetic probability theory in Markov categories.

title: Quantum Error Management in Practice: A Cross-Stack Benchmark
summary: Quantum processors have crossed the one-hundred-qubit mark, but noise continues to limit circuit performance, while full quantum error correction remains too costly for routine use. Error suppression and mitigation therefore play an important role in extracting value from current hardware, yet independent comparisons of commercial solutions on identical workloads and devices remain scarce. We benchmark IBM Qiskit Runtime, Q-CTRL Performance Management, and Qedma QESEM on IBM Pittsburgh, a 156-qubit IBM Quantum Heron r3 processor. For Sampler workloads, we run Bernstein-Vazirani, quantum phase estimation, GHZ-state preparation, and randomized mirror circuits with up to 100 measured qubits, comparing raw execution, IBM measurement twirling, and Q-CTRL. For Estimator workloads, we measure chain-averaged magnetization and correlation observables of an eight-layer transverse-field Ising circuit at 25, 50, and 75 qubits against an exact matrix-product-state reference, comparing IBM raw execution, IBM TREX plus twirling, Q-CTRL, and QESEM. Q-CTRL produced the best results on the three structured Sampler workloads while keeping reported QPU times within the same order as the IBM configurations. Across six Ising observable and system-size cases, aggregate mean absolute error was 0.0883 for IBM raw execution, 0.0807 for IBM TREX plus twirling, 0.0285 for Q-CTRL, and 0.0188 for QESEM. Relative to raw execution, Q-CTRL and QESEM reduced aggregate error by factors of 3.10 and 4.70, respectively, while QESEM used 7.5 to 11.1 times the reported QPU time of Q-CTRL. These results show that managed error suppression and mitigation can substantially improve current hardware performance, but with distinct accuracy and execution-time tradeoffs.

AI.tldr: This paper benchmarks three error suppression/mitigation solutions—IBM Qiskit Runtime, Q-CTRL Performance Management, and Qedma QESEM—on IBM Pittsburgh (156-qubit Heron r3 processor) using Sampler workloads (Bernstein-Vazirani, QPE, GHZ, mirror circuits) and Estimator workloads (transverse-field Ising with MPS reference). Q-CTRL performed best on structured Sampler workloads; on Estimator workloads, aggregate MAE was 0.0883 (raw), 0.0807 (IBM TREX+twirling), 0.0285 (Q-CTRL), 0.0188 (QESEM), with Q-CTRL and QESEM reducing error by factors of 3.10 and 4.70 relative to raw, at the cost of QESEM using 7.5–11.1× Q-CTRL's QPU time.
AI.motivation: Quantum processors have surpassed 100 qubits but remain noise-limited, and full quantum error correction is too costly for routine use. Error suppression and mitigation are therefore essential for extracting value from current hardware, yet independent comparisons of commercial solutions under identical workloads and devices are scarce.
AI.method: The authors benchmark three commercial solutions on a 156-qubit IBM Quantum Heron r3 processor. For Sampler workloads, they run Bernstein-Vazirani, quantum phase estimation, GHZ-state preparation, and randomized mirror circuits with up to 100 qubits, comparing raw execution, IBM measurement twirling, and Q-CTRL. For Estimator workloads, they measure chain-averaged magnetization and correlation observables of an eight-layer transverse-field Ising circuit at 25, 50, and 75 qubits against an exact matrix-product-state reference, comparing IBM raw execution, IBM TREX plus twirling, Q-CTRL, and QESEM.

On six Ising observable/system-size cases, aggregate MAE was 0.0883 (IBM raw), 0.0807 (IBM TREX+twirling), 0.0285 (Q-CTRL), and 0.0188 (QESEM). title: One Qubit Can Beat One Bit: Quantum Advantage for Post-Training Quantization
summary: One-bit post-training quantization represents each weight using only its sign, requiring all deployment contexts to share the same binary weight matrix even when their activation statistics favor different sign patterns. We study this shared-sign constraint and introduce Quantum Random Access Quantization (QRAQ). This framework encodes context-dependent signs in a quantum random-access code and retrieves them via context-matched Pauli measurements. Under an explicit fresh-copy logical readout model, QRAQ produces an unbiased, context-specific binary surrogate with a tractable shot-noise penalty. We prove a row-wise separation from shared-sign one-bit PTQ with signed per-row scales. When the optimal context-wise signs are incompatible, QRAQ achieves a strictly lower ideal reconstruction risk. We also derive finite-shot and calibrated-noise conditions under which this separation is retained. Fixed-readout quantum schemes are classically simulable, so the relevant resource in this model is measurement incompatibility rather than quantization alone. Finally, we characterize the role of scale granularity, provide finite-sample certificates, and evaluate the predicted ideal, finite-shot, noisy, and multi-context regimes in simulator experiments.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Quantum Random Access Quantization (QRAQ), a framework for one-bit post-training quantization that uses quantum random-access codes to encode context-dependent weight signs and retrieve them via Pauli measurements, overcoming the constraint that all deployment contexts must share the same binary weight matrix.
AI.motivation: Standard one-bit post-training quantization forces all deployment contexts to share a single binary weight matrix (based only on the sign of weights), even when different contexts have activation statistics that would favor different sign patterns. This shared-sign constraint is suboptimal.
AI.method: QRAQ encodes context-dependent signs in a quantum random-access code and retrieves them via context-matched Pauli measurements. It uses a fresh-copy logical readout model producing unbiased, context-specific binary surrogates with tractable shot-noise penalties. The framework includes finite-shot and calibrated-noise conditions, scale granularity characterization, and finite-sample certificates.
AI.result: The paper proves a row-wise separation from shared-sign one-bit PTQ with signed per-row scales: when optimal context-wise signs are incompatible, QRAQ achieves strictly lower ideal reconstruction risk. It also derives conditions under which this separation is retained with finite shots and noise. Fixed-readout quantum schemes are classically simulable, indicating measurement incompatibility (not quantization alone) is the key resource. Simulator experiments validate predicted ideal, finite-shot, noisy, and multi-context regimes.
AI.conclusion: QRAQ demonstrates that quantum random-access codes can be leveraged to break the shared-sign constraint in one-bit post-training quantization, with provable reconstruction-risk advantages in incompatible multi-context settings, and that measurement incompatibility is the fundamental resource enabling this gain.

title: Cluster-State Witnesses of Finite-Speed Hidden Influences
summary: Bell experiments rule out local common-cause explanations of quantum correlations, yet they do not exclude hidden influences that travel faster than light while still having a finite speed in a preferred frame. Multipartite spacetime arrangements turn this possibility into a constraint: two late parties that are outside each other's hidden-influence cones must remain Bell-local once the earlier events are fixed. Here, we formulate this constraint as a projected-polytope separation problem for cluster-state correlations, using only marginal data containing at most one late party. From linear cluster states, we construct a four-qubit witness with the bound $S_4\le 6$ and quantum value $4+2\sqrt2$, and a five-qubit witness with $S_5\le 10$ and quantum value $6+4\sqrt2$. We certify that the exposed faces are facets of the corresponding projected hidden-influence polytopes. These results identify linear-cluster graph states as certifiable and experimentally friendly resources for finite-speed hidden-influence tests.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a method to test finite-speed hidden-influence (superluminal) models using multipartite Bell experiments. It formulates the constraint as a projected-polytope separation problem and constructs four-qubit and five-qubit witnesses based on linear cluster states, with certified facet-exposing bounds.
AI.motivation: Standard Bell experiments rule out local causal explanations of quantum correlations but do not exclude hidden influences that propagate superluminally at finite speed in a preferred frame. The authors aim to design practical, experimentally friendly tests that can certify and constrain such finite-speed hidden-influence models.
AI.method: The constraint on finite-speed hidden influences is formulated as a projected-polytope separation problem using marginal data with at most one late party. Linear cluster states are used to construct Bell-like witnesses: a four-qubit witness with bound S4≤6 and quantum value 4+2√2, and a five-qubit witness with S5≤10 and quantum value 6+4√2. The exposed faces are certified as facets of the corresponding projected hidden-influence polytopes.
AI.result: The constructed witnesses demonstrate quantum violations of the finite-speed hidden-influence bounds, and the exposed faces are proven to be facets of the projected hidden-influence polytopes, certifying the tightness of the inequalities.
AI.conclusion: Linear-cluster graph states are identified as certifiable and experimentally friendly resources for testing finite-speed hidden-influence models, providing a practical route to go beyond standard Bell nonlocality tests.

title: Relative entropy of entanglement of Haar random states
summary: We determine the relative entropy of entanglement of a bipartite mixed state $ρ_{AB}$ obtained by tracing out one subsystem of a tripartite Haar-random pure state $|ψ\rangle_{ABC}$, finding $E_R(ρ_{AB})=\log\frac{d_Ad_B}{\max(d_A,d_B,d_C)}+O(1)$. Equivalently, the relative entropy of entanglement nearly saturates the smaller of the entanglement of formation $E_F(ρ_{AB})$ and the mutual information $I(A:B)$. The upper bound is achieved by an explicit separable state obtained through one-sided Schmidt dephasing, which is therefore approximately closest.

AI.tldr: The paper determines the relative entropy of entanglement for a bipartite mixed state obtained by tracing out one subsystem of a tripartite Haar-random pure state, showing it equals log(d_A d_B / max(d_A,d_B,d_C)) + O(1), nearly saturating the smaller of entanglement of formation and mutual information.
AI.motivation: To characterize the entanglement properties of typical (Haar-random) pure states restricted to a bipartite subsystem, and to determine how the relative entropy of entanglement behaves for such generic states.
AI.method: The authors compute the relative entropy of entanglement analytically for states formed by tracing out one party of a tripartite Haar-random pure state, using one-sided Schmidt dephasing to construct an explicit separable state that achieves the upper bound.
AI.result: The relative entropy of entanglement equals log(d_A d_B / max(d_A,d_B,d_C)) + O(1), which nearly saturates the smaller of the entanglement of formation and the mutual information. An explicit separable state via one-sided Schmidt dephasing achieves the upper bound, making it approximately the closest separable state.
AI.conclusion: For generic tripartite pure states, the restricted bipartite mixed state has a relative entropy of entanglement that is asymptotically determined by the dimension parameters, and the closest separable state can be explicitly constructed via one-sided Schmidt dephasing.

title: Scalable Circuit Cutting: A Framework for Combined Gate and Wire Cuts Using Gate Groups
summary: Quantum circuit cutting enables the execution of large circuits on devices with a limited number of qubits by partitioning circuits into independent subcircuits. However, this introduces a sampling overhead, which grows exponentially with the number of cuts, rendering the choice of cut placements critical for practical circuit cutting. Determining optimal cut placements remains computationally challenging, particularly as circuits grow in size. Additionally, existing circuit cutting approaches typically treat gate and wire cuts independently. Those combining both cutting approaches, however, do not take advantage of joint cutting, i.e., identifying common gate groups and cutting them jointly for a reduced overhead. This work presents a unified framework that combines gate and wire cutting within a single partitioning strategy, enabling more efficient circuit decompositions. Moreover, our approach incorporates joint cutting via a novel gate grouping technique, further reducing sampling overhead. By formulating the cut placement problem as a scalable graph partitioning task, our method efficiently identifies near-optimal cut placements for large circuits, also providing diagnostic feedback on whether circuits are suitable for cutting.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a unified framework for quantum circuit cutting that combines gate and wire cutting in a single partitioning strategy, incorporating joint cutting via gate grouping to reduce sampling overhead, and formulates cut placement as a scalable graph partitioning problem for near-optimal solutions on large circuits.
AI.motivation: Circuit cutting enables running large circuits on limited-qubit devices, but the sampling overhead grows exponentially with the number of cuts, making optimal cut placement critical. Existing approaches treat gate and wire cutting independently, and those that combine them do not exploit joint cutting (identifying common gate groups and cutting them together to reduce overhead).
AI.method: The approach formulates cut placement as a scalable graph partitioning problem, combining gate and wire cutting within a single partitioning strategy. It introduces a novel gate grouping technique for joint cutting, which identifies common gate groups and cuts them jointly to further reduce sampling overhead.
AI.result: The method efficiently identifies near-optimal cut placements for large circuits with reduced sampling overhead compared to existing approaches, and provides diagnostic feedback on whether circuits are suitable for cutting.
AI.conclusion: A unified partitioning framework for quantum circuit cutting that integrates gate and wire cutting with joint gate grouping yields more efficient circuit decompositions and scalable near-optimal cut placement, including diagnostic insights for practical applicability.

title: Identifying slow relaxation in many-body quantum systems through state-graph geometry and state-graph heterogeneity
summary: We adapt tools from the theory of quantum random walks to investigate slow relaxation dynamics through the many-body state graph. Specifically, we construct a probe of heterogeneity between basis states defined using hitting times derived from the unitary time-evolution operator. We find that the state-graph geometry, encoded by the pairwise hitting time of basis states, is a highly sensitive indicator of slow relaxation dynamics in a variety of systems. We study three paradigmatic models: the Rosenzweig-Porter model, the quantum East model, and the triangular lattice gas model, exhibiting a sudden onset of slow dynamics upon tuning of a control parameter. As a global characterization of the graph geometry, we analyze the spectral radius of the hitting matrix. We find that it increases sharply at the onset of slow dynamics, spanning many orders of magnitude, with a characteristic crossing point at the transition. Our work provides a geometric framework for describing and identifying phases with slow relaxation using a unified graph-theoretic formalism.

AI.tldr: The paper adapts quantum random walk tools to study slow relaxation dynamics via many-body state graph geometry, using hitting times derived from unitary time-evolution to probe heterogeneity between basis states. Applied to three models (Rosenzweig-Porter, quantum East, triangular lattice gas), the authors find that pairwise hitting times and the spectral radius of the hitting matrix sharply increase at the onset of slow dynamics, providing a unified graph-theoretic framework for identifying phases with slow relaxation.
AI.motivation: To develop a unified geometric framework for describing and identifying phases with slow relaxation dynamics across different many-body systems, using tools from quantum random walk theory.
AI.method: The authors construct a probe of heterogeneity between basis states using hitting times derived from the unitary time-evolution operator. They encode the state-graph geometry via pairwise hitting times and analyze the spectral radius of the hitting matrix as a global characterization of the graph geometry.
AI.result: The pairwise hitting time of basis states is a highly sensitive indicator of slow relaxation. The spectral radius of the hitting matrix increases sharply at the onset of slow dynamics, spanning many orders of magnitude with a characteristic crossing point at the transition, across all three studied models.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a geometric, graph-theoretic formalism to describe and identify phases with slow relaxation, offering a unified framework applicable across diverse many-body systems.

title: Quantum channel learning with limited parallel access
summary: Quantum channels can characterized by their action on an orthogonal operator basis, where these operators are related to observable properties of the quantum system. For qudit and multimode bosonic systems, this is encoded respectively in the Heisenberg--Weyl transfer matrix estimated from the Choi state, and in the characteristic-function transfer function estimated from the Choi state generated by probing with a two-mode squeezed vacuum state. We derive sample-complexity bounds for estimating entries of these transfer matrix/function to additive accuracy $ε$ with success probability $\geq1-δ$, under different resources: access to the complex-conjugate channel $\mathcal{E}^*$ and/or simultaneous access to $c$ copies of the channel. In all settings, the learner uses parallel channel calls with adaptively chosen, ancilla-assisted input states and measurements. Absolute values of transfer-matrix entries can be learned efficiently with simultaneous access to $\mathcal{E}$ and $\mathcal{E}^*$, with tight scaling $ε^{-4}$. Without conjugate access, any $c<d$ copies are insufficient for efficient learning, requiring sample complexity exponential in the number of ($d$-level) qudits $n$ (for prime $d$). Efficiency is recovered at $c=d$, with tight scaling $ε^{-2d}$. For bosonic systems, exponential sample complexity persists for all $c=O(1/ε)$. Although the task is learning a particular state, these bounds carry stronger implications than standard state-learning bounds since the learner controls the inputs and ancillary assistance. This establishes a hierarchy of channel-learning resources: self-complex-conjugate channels require two-copy ancilla-assisted access for efficient learning, while for every square-free $d$, some channels require $d$-copy access. As a corollary, we bounds tighter lower bounds for state learning with limited multi-copy access.

AI.tldr: The paper derives sample-complexity bounds for learning quantum channel transfer matrices/functions (Heisenberg-Weyl and characteristic-function) to additive accuracy ε with probability ≥1-δ, under different resource settings (conjugate channel access, c-copy simultaneous access). Key results: efficient learning with ε⁻⁴ scaling when both ε and ε* are accessible; exponential sample complexity for c<d copies (qudits); efficiency recovered at c=d with ε⁻²ᵈ scaling; exponential complexity persists for bosonic systems with c=O(1/ε). Establishes a hierarchy of channel-learning resources.
AI.motivation: To understand the fundamental sample complexity required to learn quantum channels, characterized via their action on orthogonal operator bases, and to establish which resources (conjugate channel access, multiple copies, ancilla assistance) enable efficient estimation of the transfer matrix/function entries.
AI.method: The authors analyze two channel characterizations: (1) Heisenberg-Weyl transfer matrices estimated from Choi states for qudit systems, and (2) characteristic-function transfer functions from Choi states probed via two-mode squeezed vacuum states for bosonic systems. They derive rigorous sample-complexity bounds for entry estimation under different resource settings: access to channel ε and its complex conjugate ε*, and/or simultaneous access to c copies of the channel, using parallel calls with adaptively chosen ancilla-assisted input states and measurements.
AI.result: Tight scaling ε⁻⁴ is achieved for learning absolute values of transfer-matrix entries with simultaneous access to both ε and ε*. Without conjugate access, c<d copies (for prime-dimensional qudits) yield exponential sample complexity in n, while c=d recovers efficiency with tight ε⁻²ᵈ scaling. Bosonic systems exhibit exponential complexity for all c=O(1/ε). This yields tighter lower bounds for state learning with limited multi-copy access and establishes a resource hierarchy: self-complex-conjugate channels need two-copy ancilla-assisted access, while some channels for every square-free d require d-copy access.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes a fundamental hierarchy of quantum channel-learning resources, showing that conjugate channel access or sufficient multi-copy access are necessary and sufficient for efficient learning, with precise scaling exponents. The findings have corollary implications for state learning with limited multi-copy access.

title: Unidirectional Dark-to-Bright Rescue in Cavity-Coupled Quantum Transport
summary: Strong light-matter coupling in optical microcavities can transport energy ballistically across an emitter array, but the same coupling buries most of the excitation in a manifold of dark states that grows with system size and traps energy outside the transport channel. We show that the off-diagonal (non-Condon) part of the exciton-phonon coupling opens a one-way escape route from this trap, driving population irreversibly from dark states into the radiative channel. This rate is fixed by a photonic-weight conservation law rather than by dark-bright overlap which evacuates the dark manifold at a rate independent of system size. The mechanism contributes to transport with near-complete efficiency with four signatures being single exponential dark state decay, a size scaling efficiency gap, distinct temperature behavior, and a resonance in the escape rate at vibrational bath modes. Beyond polariton transport, it recasts dark states from a parasitic loss channel into an engineered dissipative resource, with implications for light harvesting and dissipation based quantum control.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that the off-diagonal (non-Condon) exciton-phonon coupling provides a one-way escape route from dark states into the radiative channel in strongly coupled optical microcavities, enabling near-complete efficiency of ballistic energy transport that is independent of system size.
AI.motivation: Strong light-matter coupling enables ballistic energy transport across emitter arrays, but most excitation energy is trapped in dark states whose population grows with system size, blocking transport efficiency. The goal is to understand and exploit a mechanism that can evacuate the dark manifold effectively.
AI.method: The authors analyze the off-diagonal (non-Condon) part of the exciton-phonon coupling and show it opens a one-way irreversible pathway from dark states into the radiative channel, governed by a photonic-weight conservation law that decouples the escape rate from dark-bright overlap.
AI.result: The mechanism evacuates the dark manifold at a rate independent of system size, achieving near-complete transport efficiency. Four signatures identify the process: single exponential dark state decay, a size-scaling efficiency gap, distinct temperature dependence, and a resonance in the escape rate at vibrational bath modes.
AI.conclusion: The findings recast dark states from a parasitic loss channel into an engineered dissipative resource, with broader implications for light harvesting and dissipation-based quantum control beyond polariton transport.

title: Machine learning for sample-based quantum diagonalization: generative configuration recovery and the classical-simulability frontier
comment: 30 pages, 10 figures. Review. Code and a reproducible notebook: https://github.com/nicolasbonilla/ml-for-sqd-review
summary: Sample-based quantum diagonalization (SQD), equivalently quantum-selected configuration interaction (QSCI), has in two years become a pragmatic centre of gravity of pre-fault-tolerant quantum chemistry: a quantum processor samples electronic configurations, and the many-electron Hamiltonian is diagonalized classically in the resulting determinant subspace. Its accuracy is set entirely by which configurations enter that subspace, a selection problem for machine learning made acute by a coupon-collector bottleneck. We critically review the ecosystem of generative and learned selectors, organizing it by the object each method generates and the importance signal it exploits, and expose one conspicuous gap: a reward-proportional generative-flow-network proposer built for tail discovery. We then confront the field's central question -- whether the quantum sampler beats classical selected configuration interaction -- and report a carefully scoped negative: across published same-active-space comparisons, strong classical selected CI matches or beats the quantum-sampled subspace, and the flagship single-layer circuits now admit polynomial-time classical energy estimation. We distil a benchmarking standard and turn the negative into a regime map, then test it with FCI-exact experiments that confirm one prediction and refute another: the cheap prior's rank correlation with the exact weights declines with multireference character (a usable coordinate), but a controlled single-molecule noise sweep shows the one generative advantage we find, robustness to valid-shot starvation, to be generic rather than the multireference-specific effect a confounded contrast first suggested. Finally, we flag learning from quantum experiments, whose classical sample-complexity lower bound is an unconditional theorem, as the one adjacent frontier where a quantum advantage is provable but not yet bridged to chemistry.

AI.tldr: This paper critically reviews sample-based quantum diagonalization (SQD/QSCI) for pre-fault-tolerant quantum chemistry, focusing on how electronic configurations are selected for the classical diagonalization subspace. It exposes a gap in selector design (reward-proportional generative-flow networks), reports a carefully scoped negative result—strong classical selected CI matches or beats quantum-sampled subspaces—derives a benchmarking regime map, tests its predictions with FCI-exact experiments (one confirmed, one refuted), and flags learning from quantum experiments as a provably advantageous frontier not yet bridged to chemistry.
AI.motivation: SQD/QSCI has become a central pragmatic method in pre-fault-tolerant quantum chemistry, but its accuracy is entirely determined by which configurations enter the classical diagonalization subspace. The configuration selection problem suffers from a coupon-collector bottleneck, making it a critical and insufficiently understood problem worth systematic review and benchmarking.
AI.method: The authors critically review the ecosystem of generative and learned selectors for SQD, organizing methods by what object they generate and what importance signal they exploit. They expose a gap: reward-proportional generative-flow-network proposers for tail discovery. They design a benchmarking standard and regime map, and test it with FCI-exact experiments including a controlled single-molecule noise sweep to disentangle confounded variables.
AI.result: Across published same-active-space comparisons, strong classical selected CI matches or beats the quantum-sampled subspace; flagship single-layer circuits admit polynomial-time classical energy estimation. FCI-exact experiments confirm that the cheap prior's rank correlation with exact weights declines with multireference character (a usable coordinate), but refute that generative robustness to valid-shot starvation is multireference-specific—it is generic, as shown by a controlled noise sweep.
AI.conclusion: The paper delivers a structured negative result (classical selected CI is competitive), a calibrated regime map and benchmarking standard for the field, and identifies learning-from-quantum-experiments as the one adjacent frontier where quantum advantage is provable (via an unconditional sampling-complexity lower bound) but not yet connected to chemistry.

title: The Hidden Subgroup Problem in Semidirect Products and Quasi-Hamiltonian Groups
summary:
Several early quantum algorithms, including Simon's algorithm and Shor's period-finding are instances of the hidden subgroup problem (HSP) over finite abelian groups. No polynomial-time quantum algorithm is known for the HSP over arbitrary non-abelian finite groups. The non-Abelian case is of particular interest because some instances, such as the dihedral and symmetric group HSPs, are connected to lattice problems and graph isomorphism, respectively.
  In this work, we give polynomial-time quantum algorithms for two further families containing non-Abelian groups. First, we consider groups of the form $G=A\rtimes_{\varphi} \mathbb{Z}_{p^k}$, with $A$ finite Abelian, $p$ prime, $k\in \mathbb{N}$ and the action of $\mathbb Z_{p^k}$ is generated by the scalar automorphism $a\mapstoμa$, for some $μ\in\mathbb Z_{\operatorname{Exp}(A)}^\times$, where $\mathrm{Exp}(A)$ is the exponent of $A$. Our algorithm is efficient when $A$ has bounded generator rank and $\mathrm{Exp}(A)/p=\mathrm{polylog}(|G|)$. This includes the case $A=\mathbb{Z}_N$ for $N\in\mathbb{N}$ and $k=1$, studied by Bacon, Childs and van Dam (FOCS 2005), and $A=\mathbb{Z}_{q^r}$ with $q$ prime and $r\in \mathbb{N}$ studied by van Dam and Dey (TQC 2014). Second, we give a polynomial-time quantum algorithm for finite quasi-Hamiltonian groups under a mild assumption on the input structure. Quasi-Hamiltonian groups are finite nilpotent groups with modular subgroup lattice, or equivalently the finite groups in which every subgroup is permutable. As far as we know, this is the first quantum algorithm to exploit the modularity of the subgroup lattice for solving the HSP. This extends, under the aforementioned structured input assumption, the quantum algorithm for Dedekind groups given by Hallgren, Russell, and Ta-Shma (SIAM J. Comput. 32, 2003).

AI.tldr: The paper gives polynomial-time quantum algorithms for the hidden subgroup problem (HSP) over two new families of non-abelian finite groups: (1) semidirect products G = A ⋊ Z_{p^k} where A is finite abelian and the action is a scalar multiplication automorphism, and (2) finite quasi-Hamiltonian groups (nilpotent groups with modular subgroup lattice) under a mild structural input assumption. These extend prior results for metacyclic-like groups (Bacon-Childs-van Dam, van Dam-Dey) and for Dedekind groups (Hallgren-Russell-Ta-Shma).
AI.motivation: The hidden subgroup problem over arbitrary finite non-abelian groups has no known polynomial-time quantum algorithm, yet specific non-abelian cases are deeply connected to important computational problems: the dihedral HSP relates to lattice problems and the symmetric HSP to graph isomorphism. This work is motivated by expanding the class of non-abelian groups for which efficient quantum algorithms exist, thereby narrowing the gap toward resolving these outstanding connections.
AI.method: The algorithms leverage the structure of the two group families. For semidirect products G = A ⋊_φ Z_{p^k} with scalar automorphism action a↦μa, the algorithm is efficient when A has bounded generator rank and Exp(A)/p = polylog(|G|). For quasi-Hamiltonian groups, which are finite nilpotent groups with modular subgroup lattice, the algorithm exploits the modularity of the subgroup lattice (a structural property not previously used for the HSP), under a mild assumption on the input structure. Both build on and extend prior techniques from Bacon-Childs-van Dam and van Dam-Dey for abelian-HSP instances, and Hallgren-Russell-Ta-Shma for Dedekind groups.
AI.result: The first algorithm handles groups A ⋊_φ Z_{p^k} with scalar automorphism action and given efficiency conditions, subsuming and generalizing the cases A = Z_N, k=1 (Bacon-Childs-van Dam) and A = Z_{q^r} (van Dam-Dey). The second algorithm provides a polynomial-time quantum HSP solver for finite quasi-Hamiltonian groups under a mild structured input assumption, extending the Dedekind group algorithm of Hallgren-Russell-Ta-Shma to this broader class.
AI.conclusion: The paper presents the first quantum algorithms exploiting modularity of the subgroup lattice, adding quasi-Hamiltonian groups to the growing class of non-abelian groups for which the HSP can be solved in polynomial time, and broadens the semidirect-product family using scalar automorphisms under stated efficiency conditions. These results advance the ongoing search for efficient quantum HSP algorithms just outside the abelian and Dedekind settings.

title: QBism on Locality and Nonlocality
summary: Recently Pienaar (2026), building on work of Cavalcanti (2021), has shown that QBism cannot always assume distinct observers' quantum-measurement outcomes---say, of Wigner and his friend---are embedded in a single spacetime. This follows from QBism's rejection of the `Absoluteness of Observed Events' assumption in the Bong et al. no-go theorem. Thus, QBism has no choice but to treat the notion of spacetime every bit as personalistic as it treats quantum states and quantum measurement outcomes. In a way, this is not a surprise to QBists, as they have taken the notion of `personalist spacetimes' to be the ansatz most compatible with their other views since at least 2009. But it does enjoin us to finally make crystal clear the sense in which QBism is a purely local interpretation of quantum mechanics despite this new theorem and despite quantum theory's age-old violation of Bell's inequalities. With the extra clarity we also hope to poise QBism for a distinctly new way to approach issues at the interface of quantum theory and gravity.

AI.tldr: Building on recent work showing QBism must treat spacetime as personalistic (like quantum states), this paper clarifies how QBism remains a purely local interpretation of quantum mechanics despite the Wigner's-friend no-go theorems and Bell violations, positioning QBism for new approaches at the quantum-gravity interface.
AI.motivation: Recent work (Pienaar 2026, building on Cavalcanti 2021) shows QBism cannot assume distinct observers' measurement outcomes are embedded in a single spacetime, due to QBism's rejection of the 'Absoluteness of Observed Events' assumption. This forces a clarification of how QBism can be local despite this and despite Bell violations.
AI.method: The paper argues through the implications of the Bong et al. no-go theorem for QBism, specifically building on the fact that QBism rejects the Absoluteness of Observed Events assumption. It connects this to the existing notion of 'personalist spacetimes' that QBists have held since 2009.
AI.result: The analysis makes crystal clear the sense in which QBism is a purely local interpretation of quantum mechanics, despite the Wigner's-friend theorem and Bell inequality violations, and positions QBism for new approaches to quantum-gravity interface issues.
AI.conclusion: QBism must treat spacetime itself as personalistic, consistent with its treatment of quantum states and outcomes. This clarifies QBism's locality and opens a new pathway for addressing quantum theory and gravity.

title: Maximally entangled states are not complete for pseudo-telepathy
summary: One of the longstanding open problems in quantum nonlocality is to determine if maximally entangled states are complete for bipartite pseudo-telepathic games: namely, if every nonlocal game which admits a perfect entangled strategy admits such a strategy which uses a maximally entangled state. We exhibit a counterexample to this in the form of a bipartite nonlocal game with input sets of size 4 and 3 and output sets both of size 6. This game is part of a new class of nonlocal games, which we call inner product games, which could be of independent interest.

AI.tldr: The paper addresses an open problem in quantum nonlocality: whether maximally entangled states are complete for bipartite pseudo-telepathic games. The authors provide a counterexample—a bipartite nonlocal game with input sets of sizes 4 and 3, output sets both of size 6—that admits a perfect entangled strategy but not one using a maximally entangled state. This game belongs to a new class called "inner product games," which may be of independent interest.
AI.motivation: The work tackles a longstanding open problem in quantum nonlocality: determining whether every nonlocal game with a perfect entangled strategy can be played perfectly using a maximally entangled state. Settling this question is fundamental to understanding the structure of quantum correlations and the power of entanglement in pseudo-telepathic games.
AI.method: The authors construct a counterexample using a new class of bipartite nonlocal games called "inner product games." They define a specific game instance with input sets of size 4 and 3, and output sets both of size 6, then demonstrate that while a perfect entangled strategy exists, no such strategy can employ a maximally entangled state.
AI.result: The authors exhibit a bipartite nonlocal game that serves as a counterexample to the conjecture that maximally entangled states are complete for bipartite pseudo-telepathic games. The game has small input/output dimensions (4×3 inputs, 6×6 outputs) and belongs to the new class of inner product games.
AI.conclusion: The answer to the open problem is negative: maximally entangled states are not complete for bipartite pseudo-telepathic games. The introduced inner product games class may provide a useful framework for further studying nonlocal games and quantum correlations.

title: Quantum Error Mitigation with Diffusion-Like Models
summary: Coupling between a quantum system and its environment causes decoherence by transferring information from the system to environmental degrees of freedom. When discretized in time, such interactions can be interpreted as sequences of weak measurements that provide an effective model of noisy quantum dynamics. Motivated by this picture, we propose an AI-assisted error-mitigation framework for quantum diffusion processes generated by sequential local weak measurements. The forward process progressively erases information from the input state through weak measurements performed in randomly selected Pauli bases, producing basis-dependent local dephasing and locally depolarizing dynamics on average. Machine-learning models are trained on exact synthetic density matrices to learn a channel- and distribution-specific denoising map and estimate the corresponding pre-noise state. We benchmark the approach on single-qubit states and separable and entangled multi-qubit registers. We also study distribution-dependent local-to-global reconstruction, in which local reduced density matrices are used to reconstruct the global state. This experimentally motivated setting relies on locally accessible information and is therefore compatible with noisy and distributed quantum systems. More broadly, the framework provides a hybrid classical-quantum approach for approximating non-unitary dynamics and mitigating coherence loss.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an AI-assisted error-mitigation framework for quantum diffusion processes induced by sequential local weak measurements. Machine learning models are trained on synthetic density matrices to learn denoising maps that estimate pre-noise states, benchmarked on single-qubit and multi-qubit systems, including a local-to-global reconstruction approach compatible with noisy distributed quantum systems.
AI.motivation: Quantum systems inevitably couple to their environment, causing decoherence through information transfer to environmental degrees of freedom. Discretized interactions can be modeled as sequences of weak measurements, providing an effective model of noisy quantum dynamics. The authors aim to develop a practical error-mitigation approach for such quantum diffusion processes that uses machine learning to undo noise effects.
AI.method: The forward process progressively erases information from input states via weak measurements in randomly selected Pauli bases, generating basis-dependent local dephasing and locally depolarizing dynamics on average. Machine-learning models are trained on exact synthetic density matrices to learn channel- and distribution-specific denoising maps. The framework includes a distribution-dependent local-to-global reconstruction, where local reduced density matrices are used to reconstruct the global state.
AI.result: The approach is benchmarked on single-qubit states, separable multi-qubit states, and entangled multi-qubit registers. The local-to-global reconstruction setting relies on locally accessible information, making it compatible with noisy and distributed quantum systems.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a hybrid classical-quantum approach for approximating non-unitary dynamics and mitigating coherence loss, offering a practical avenue for error mitigation in quantum systems.

title: Feasibility-Preserving Quantum Search for Constrained Transportation Routing
summary: Transportation routing problems such as the Traveling Salesperson Problem (TSP) and the Vehicle Routing Problem (VRP) are characterized by strict feasibility requirements involving customer assignment and visit rules, route sequencing, and depot-return logic alongside cost minimization. Most quantum routing formulations adopt Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization (QUBO) encodings, where feasibility is incorporated indirectly via penalty terms in the cost Hamiltonian. While convenient for standard implementations of the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA), QUBO encodings allow the quantum search dynamics to allocate substantial probability to infeasible route configurations. This study develops a transportation-grounded constraint-aware Quantum Alternating Operator Ansatz (QAOA+) framework that embeds feasibility-preserving logic directly into the search operator. We introduce a custom mixer that functions as a quantum analogue of feasibility-preserving routing neighborhoods, using column-wise swap moves, it restricts evolution to feasible configurations while enabling structured exploration of valid routes. We compare three constraint-handling architectures: penalty-based QUBO QAOA, penalty free QAOA+ with the feasibility-preserving mixer, and a Hybrid QAOA+ combining mixer based feasibility with and penalty guidance. Results on small TSP and VRP instances show that constraint-handling architecture strongly influences feasible-route sampling, convergence behavior, and probability concentration over low-cost feasible routes. These findings position constraint-aware quantum search as a methodological extension of transportation routing search approaches, where feasibility is enforced through admissible quantum transitions rather than post-hoc penalties.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a constraint-aware Quantum Alternating Operator Ansatz (QAOA+) framework for transportation routing problems (TSP and VRP), introducing a custom feasibility-preserving mixer based on column-wise swap moves that restricts quantum evolution to valid routes. It compares three constraint-handling architectures—penalty-based QUBO QAOA, penalty-free QAOA+, and a hybrid approach—showing that the constraint-handling strategy significantly impacts feasible-route sampling, convergence, and probability concentration on low-cost feasible solutions.
AI.motivation: Standard QUBO encodings for TSP/VRP incorporate feasibility only via penalty terms, allowing quantum search to allocate substantial probability mass to infeasible route configurations. This undermines the efficiency and reliability of quantum optimization for transportation routing, motivating the need for feasibility-preserving search operators.
AI.method: The authors develop a QAOA+ framework with a custom mixer operating as a quantum analogue of feasibility-preserving routing neighborhoods. The mixer uses column-wise swap moves to restrict evolution to feasible configurations while enabling structured exploration of valid routes. Three architectures are compared: (1) penalty-based QUBO QAOA, (2) penalty-free QAOA+ with the feasibility-preserving mixer, and (3) a hybrid QAOA+ combining mixer-based feasibility with penalty guidance.
AI.result: Experiments on small TSP and VRP instances demonstrate that the choice of constraint-handling architecture strongly influences feasible-route sampling, convergence behavior, and probability concentration over low-cost feasible routes, with the QAOA+ feasibility-preserving approaches showing advantages over penalty-based QUBO formulations.
AI.conclusion: Constraint-aware quantum search constitutes a methodological extension of transportation routing search, where feasibility is enforced through admissible quantum transitions (embedded in the search operator) rather than post-hoc penalties. This positions the approach as a promising direction for quantum-native routing optimization.

title: Interferometric Quantum Polynomial Chaos Expansion as a Generative Model for Calorimeter Shower Simulation
summary: We present the quantum polynomial chaos expansion, a generative algorithm in which a single circuit is the entire model, and we use it to learn calorimeter images. In a classical chaos expansion the randomness is the input and the coefficients are fitted. Here the randomness is still the only input, entering the circuit as rotation angles and re-uploaded at every block, so that each measured observable is a chaos expansion of the latent variables whose order equals the circuit depth, and what is fitted are the gate angles themselves. Expressivity therefore grows with depth rather than with classical coefficients, correlations between outputs arise only from entangling gates, and a single latent wire read by all qubits carries the collective mode of the data. Nothing fitted stands between the circuit and the sample, so switching the entanglers off is a setting of the model itself and provably yields independent outputs, and attribution of the learned correlations to individual gates becomes a measurement. Choosing between two measurement bases shot by shot sharpens attribution into certification, and the trained model violates the Bell bound obeyed by every classical generative model with local response, whatever its size. We train the model on Geant4 shower data, execute the identical circuit on a superconducting processor with its accuracy loss predicted in advance, prove a no-go theorem for the tail dependence of every smooth generator read out through expectation values, and identify the circuit primitive that removes this limit.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces quantum polynomial chaos expansion, a generative algorithm where a single quantum circuit serves as the entire model, trained on calorimeter shower images. The randomness enters as rotation angles re-uploaded at every block, making each measured observable a chaos expansion whose order equals circuit depth, with gate angles as the fitted parameters. The model is trained on Geant4 data, executed on a superconducting processor with predicted accuracy loss, and shown to violate Bell bounds that constrain all classical generative models with local response.
AI.motivation: To develop a generative model whose expressivity grows with circuit depth rather than classical coefficients, where correlations between outputs arise only from entangling gates, and where learned correlations can be attributed to individual gates as a measurement—overcoming limitations of classical generative models and enabling certified, interpretable generation of calorimeter images.
AI.method: The authors construct a quantum polynomial chaos expansion where random latent variables enter as rotation angles re-uploaded at every block of a single circuit. Measured observables are chaos expansions of latent variables with order equal to circuit depth, and gate angles are the fitted parameters. A single latent wire read by all qubits captures the collective data mode. The model supports switching off entanglers for provably independent outputs, shot-by-shot basis switching for attribution sharpening into certification, and includes a no-go theorem analysis for smooth generators read out via expectation values, plus a circuit primitive that removes this limitation.
AI.result: The model was trained on Geant4 shower data and the identical circuit was executed on a superconducting processor with accuracy loss predicted in advance. The trained model violates the Bell bound obeyed by every classical generative model with local response. A no-go theorem was proven for the tail dependence of every smooth generator read out through expectation values, and a circuit primitive was identified that removes this limit.
AI.conclusion: Quantum polynomial chaos expansion provides a generative framework where the circuit is both model and measurement, offering certifiable correlations (via Bell-style bounds), attribution of learned correlations to individual gates, and controllable independence, with demonstrated execution on real quantum hardware and a provable path beyond the tail-dependence limitations of smooth generators.

title: Qutrit entanglement and joint multi-parameter estimation in an optical clock platform
summary: Quantum metrology harnesses entanglement to improve measurement precision beyond classical limits. While standard protocols rely on two-level qubits to estimate a single parameter, extending them to entangled multi-level qudits enables the optimal simultaneous estimation of multiple parameters within a single probe. However, generating such multi-level entanglement and harnessing it for joint multi-parameter estimation in atomic clocks has remained an outstanding challenge. Here, we experimentally demonstrate genuine qutrit entanglement and joint multi-parameter estimation in an optical clock platform. Leveraging control over the ground state and two fine-structure clock states of $^{88}\text{Sr}$ atoms trapped in triple-magic optical tweezers, we generate a maximally entangled two-qutrit state with a loss-postselected fidelity of F = 0.85(1), certifying genuine multi-level entanglement. Taking advantage of this high-dimensional entanglement, we theoretically construct and experimentally realize an optimal two-qutrit metrological probe state and noise-robust readout circuit to simultaneously estimate injected phases on two optical clock transitions. We observe a joint estimation variance below the ideal individual two-level sensing threshold, and show theoretically that this advantage persists at state-of-the-art atom numbers under circuit-level noise. These results demonstrate the key building blocks towards quantum information science with high-dimensional states encoded in the internal energy levels of neutral atoms.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates genuine qutrit entanglement and joint multi-parameter estimation in an optical clock platform using 88Sr atoms trapped in triple-magic optical tweezers, achieving a maximally entangled two-qutrit state with fidelity F=0.85(1) and demonstrating simultaneous phase estimation on two optical clock transitions below the classical two-level sensing threshold.
AI.motivation: Standard quantum metrology protocols use two-level qubits to estimate a single parameter, but extending to entangled multi-level qudits enables optimal simultaneous estimation of multiple parameters within a single probe. Generating multi-level entanglement and harnessing it for joint multi-parameter estimation in atomic clocks has remained an outstanding challenge.
AI.method: Using 88Sr atoms trapped in triple-magic optical tweezers with control over the ground state and two fine-structure clock states, the authors generate a maximally entangled two-qutrit state. They theoretically construct and experimentally realize an optimal two-qutrit metrological probe state with a noise-robust readout circuit to simultaneously estimate injected phases on two optical clock transitions.
AI.result: They achieve a loss-postselected fidelity of F=0.85(1) certifying genuine multi-level (qutrit) entanglement, and observe a joint estimation variance below the ideal individual two-level sensing threshold. Theoretical analysis shows this advantage persists at state-of-the-art atom numbers under circuit-level noise.
AI.conclusion: These results demonstrate key building blocks towards quantum information science with high-dimensional states encoded in the internal energy levels of neutral atoms, establishing atomic clock platforms as viable systems for high-dimensional quantum metrology.

title: Experimental demonstration of the Quantum Fourier Transform on up to 100 qubits using a convolutional compilation strategy
summary: We present and experimentally validate the `Convolutional QFT': a constructive compilation strategy for the Quantum Fourier Transform (QFT) subroutine on a linear nearest neighbor (LNN) qubit topology. We first introduce a novel strategy that compiles the $n$-qubit QFT onto an LNN topology using only $n^2 - n$ $CX$ gates, matching requirements of a direct compilation on an all-to-all architecture. We then derive the convolutional variant used in our experiments, which requires an additional two $CX$ gates in total, and is realized via a compact, translation-invariant kernel circuit gadget that traverses a quantum register. We demonstrate the power of the convolutional compilation strategy on the IBM Quantum Platform by executing QFT benchmarking circuits. We measure a process fidelity of 11.4% at 50 qubits, and 1.8% at 80 qubits. The correct output state remains clearly distinguishable above background noise up to 100 qubits. These results constitute the largest experimental QFT demonstrated on any quantum computing hardware to date.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the "Convolutional QFT," a constructive compilation strategy for the Quantum Fourier Transform on linear nearest neighbor (LNN) qubit topologies. It compiles the n-qubit QFT using only n²-n CX gates (matching all-to-all requirements) plus two additional CX gates for the convolutional variant. The method uses a compact, translation-invariant kernel circuit gadget that traverses the register. Experiments on IBM Quantum Platform achieved 11.4% process fidelity at 50 qubits, 1.8% at 80 qubits, with correct output distinguishable up to 100 qubits—the largest experimental QFT demonstrated to date.
AI.motivation: The QFT is a critical subroutine in many quantum algorithms, but its compilation onto realistic hardware topologies—particularly LNN architectures—has been inefficient. The authors aim to close the gap between LNN and all-to-all compilation overhead for QFT, which previously required more CX gates on restricted topologies.
AI.method: The authors derive a novel compilation strategy that maps the n-qubit QFT to LNN topology using n²-n CX gates, matching all-to-all requirements. They then introduce a convolutional variant, requiring only two additional CX gates in total, implemented via a compact translation-invariant kernel circuit that traverses the quantum register. The method was validated experimentally on IBM Quantum hardware using QFT benchmarking circuits.
AI.result: Process fidelity measured at 11.4% for 50 qubits and 1.8% for 80 qubits on IBM Quantum Platform. The correct output state remained distinguishable above background noise up to 100 qubits. These results represent the largest experimental QFT demonstrated on any quantum hardware to date.
AI.conclusion: The convolutional QFT compilation strategy achieves CX gate counts on LNN topologies that match all-to-all architectures (within two gates), demonstrating that restricted connectivity need not be a bottleneck for QFT implementation. The experimental results establish a new scale record for QFT execution on real quantum hardware.

title: What meter interference can tell us about the statistics of weak measurements
summary: It is widely assumed that the quantum fluctuations of the meter readout in a weak measurement make it impossible to identify the contributions originating from the individual values of the physical property observed in the measurement. Here, we show that a careful analysis of the quantum dynamics of the meter system allows us to identify a universal relation between quantum interference in the post-selection probability, and quantum interference in the statistics of the meter readout. The analysis reveals that quantum interference modifies the readout distribution of the meter in two ways, a diffusion term that identifies the appropriate operator ordering in the post-selected variance of the observed system property, and a wavefunction-dependent update of the initial meter statistics based on the effect of back action on the post-selection probability. Our results show that the statistical patterns described by meter interference provide important details about the physics of post-selection in weak measurements, allowing us to exclude the possibility of statistical artefacts in the experimental observation of weak values.

AI.tldr: The paper reveals a universal relation between quantum interference in post-selection probability and quantum interference in the meter readout statistics of weak measurements, showing that meter interference modifies the readout distribution via a diffusion term and a back-action-dependent update, and that these statistical patterns rule out artefacts in weak value observations.
AI.motivation: It is commonly assumed that quantum fluctuations of the meter readout in weak measurements prevent identification of contributions from individual values of the measured physical property. The authors aim to challenge this assumption by analyzing the quantum dynamics of the meter system.
AI.method: The authors perform a careful analysis of the quantum dynamics of the meter system in weak measurements, establishing a universal relation between quantum interference in post-selection probability and quantum interference in the statistics of the meter readout.
AI.result: Quantum interference modifies the meter readout distribution in two ways: (1) a diffusion term that identifies the appropriate operator ordering in the post-selected variance of the observed system property, and (2) a wavefunction-dependent update of the initial meter statistics based on the back-action effect on the post-selection probability.
AI.conclusion: The statistical patterns described by meter interference provide important details about the physics of post-selection in weak measurements, and exclude the possibility of statistical artefacts in the experimental observation of weak values.

title: Generating two-mechanical mode entangled cat states, and steady-state entanglement, in cavity optomechanics in the presence of dissipation
summary: We investigate a dissipation-engineering approach to produce a phase-dependent collective-mode Schrödinger cat state involving two modes. Our model features a single cavity mode that interacts with two spectrally identical mechanical oscillators. Both oscillators are coupled through a phase-dependent hopping interaction. We demonstrate that by adjusting the phase of the phonon-hopping interaction, one can control the bipartite entanglement of the phase-dependent two-mode cat state during its generation. Additionally, our study reveals that phonon interactions act as a tunable parameter, enabling the manipulation of steady-state entanglement between the bare mechanical modes, even in the presence of environmental effects and thermal excitations. Our scheme provides a feasible approach for the phase-dependent multi mode non-Gaussian states preparation.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a dissipation-engineering scheme to generate a phase-dependent collective-mode Schrödinger cat state using a single cavity mode coupled to two spectrally identical mechanical oscillators with phase-dependent phonon-hopping interaction. The phase of the hopping interaction controls bipartite entanglement during cat-state generation, and phonon interactions enable tunable steady-state entanglement between bare mechanical modes even under thermal noise.
AI.motivation: To produce phase-dependent multimode non-Gaussian states and control bipartite entanglement between mechanical modes via dissipation engineering and a tunable phonon-hopping phase.
AI.method: The model consists of a single cavity mode interacting with two identical mechanical oscillators coupled via a phase-dependent hopping interaction. Dissipation engineering is used to generate a phase-dependent collective-mode Schrödinger cat state, with the hopping phase serving as a control parameter for entanglement.
AI.result: The phase of the phonon-hopping interaction allows control of bipartite entanglement during generation of the two-mode cat state. Phonon interactions provide a tunable knob to manipulate steady-state entanglement between bare mechanical modes, robust against environmental effects and thermal excitations.
AI.conclusion: The scheme offers a feasible route to preparing phase-dependent multimode non-Gaussian states with controllable entanglement, including robustness under realistic thermal and environmental conditions.

title: X-Z Round Scheduling for the Surface Code with Defects under Biased Noise
summary: Fault-tolerant Quantum Computing (FTQC) relies on Quantum Error Correction (QEC) codes that encode logical qubits across many physical qubits to detect and correct errors. The surface code is among the most widely studied codes due to its high error threshold, the existence of efficient decoders, and hardware-friendly properties: a planar, two-dimensional layout with nearest-neighbor connectivity. In practice, however, the fabrication of solid-state quantum processors introduces hardware defects, resulting in defective qubits and couplers that must be discarded. Adapting the surface code to these defects often requires measuring the $X$- and $Z$-type checks in separate rounds rather than simultaneously. In this work, we investigate the optimal $X$-to-$Z$ checks round-scheduling ratio under biased noise systems. Our results characterize how key architectural parameters, such as noise bias, code distance, and defect rate, impact the logical error rate. We provide insights into how to determine the optimal scheduling ratio directly from device calibration data, enabling manufacturers to maximize performance without extensive simulations. Our approach reduces the logical error rate by up to $4.25\times$ at a $1\%$ defect rate and up to $8.46\times$ at a $2\%$ defect rate for a distance-$13$ surface code under moderately biased noise. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the benefits of round-scheduling extend beyond the defective-hardware setting. In biased-noise architectures subject to CNOT crosstalk, separating $X$ and $Z$ measurement rounds yields up to $4.5\times$ reduction in logical error rate.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates optimal X-to-Z check round-scheduling ratios in surface code quantum error correction under biased noise with defective qubits, showing significant logical error rate reductions (up to 8.46x) and providing manufacturer-friendly guidelines derived from device calibration data.
AI.motivation: Fabrication defects in solid-state quantum processors create defective qubits and couplers that complicate surface code implementation, often requiring X-type and Z-type checks to be measured in separate rounds. The optimal scheduling ratio between these rounds is not well understood, yet it significantly impacts logical error rates and depends on architectural parameters like noise bias, code distance, and defect rate.
AI.method: The authors systematically characterize how noise bias, code distance, and defect rate affect the logical error rate as a function of the X-to-Z check round-scheduling ratio. They develop insights enabling direct determination of optimal scheduling ratios from device calibration data, avoiding extensive simulations. They also extend their analysis to CNOT crosstalk scenarios in biased-noise architectures.
AI.result: The approach reduces logical error rate by up to 4.25x at 1% defect rate and up to 8.46x at 2% defect rate for a distance-13 surface code under moderately biased noise. In biased-noise architectures with CNOT crosstalk (defect-free), separating X and Z measurement rounds yields up to 4.5x reduction in logical error rate.
AI.conclusion: Optimal round-scheduling ratios can be determined directly from device calibration data, allowing manufacturers to maximize performance without extensive simulations. The benefits of round-scheduling are not limited to defective hardware but also apply to defect-free biased-noise architectures suffering from CNOT crosstalk.

title: A Unified Framework for Sample Complexity of Structured Quantum State Tomography under Noisy Observations
summary: Quantum state tomography (QST) has attracted considerable attention due to its fundamental role in quantum information processing. In this paper, we develop a unified theoretical framework for analyzing the sample complexity of structured QST under noisy observations arising from state preparation noise, measurement noise, and finite-shot statistical noise. The proposed framework applies to a broad family of structured quantum-state classes, including general mixed states, sparse states, low-rank states, matrix product states (MPSs), matrix product operators (MPOs), projected entangled-pair states (PEPSs), and projected entangled-pair operators (PEPOs), while further introducing physically consistent structured models---including low-rank and sparse states, low-rank MPOs (LR-MPOs), and low-rank PEPOs (LR-PEPOs)---that simultaneously exploit low-dimensional structures and preserve the physical constraint. Within this framework, we derive unified non-asymptotic sample complexity guarantees for two constrained least-squares estimators under noisy observations: a noise-aware estimator that incorporates the calibrated noise model and a noise-unaware estimator based on the ideal Born measurement model. For the noise-aware estimator, we derive unified trace-norm recovery guarantees that explicitly characterize the dependence of the sample complexity on three fundamental quantities: the complexity of the underlying structured state class, the complexity of the measurement ensemble, and the state preparation and measurement noise levels. For the noise-unaware estimator, we establish a unified non-asymptotic recovery guarantee consisting of a statistical error term and an additional deterministic bias term arising from the mismatch between the assumed reconstruction model and the noisy observation process.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a unified theoretical framework for analyzing the sample complexity of structured quantum state tomography (QST) under noisy observations, covering both noise-aware and noise-unaware constrained least-squares estimators, and derives non-asymptotic recovery guarantees that characterize the dependence on state-class complexity, measurement ensemble complexity, and noise levels.
AI.motivation: Quantum state tomography is fundamental to quantum information processing, but existing analyses of sample complexity are fragmented across different state classes and often ignore realistic noise sources (state preparation noise, measurement noise, and finite-shot statistical noise). A unified framework is needed to systematically understand how structure, noise, and measurements interact in determining the required number of samples.
AI.method: The authors propose a general theoretical framework applicable to a broad family of structured quantum state classes (mixed states, sparse states, low-rank states, MPSs, MPOs, PEPSs, PEPOs) and introduce physically consistent structured models (low-rank and sparse states, LR-MPOs, LR-PEPOs) that preserve physical constraints. They analyze two constrained least-squares estimators: a noise-aware estimator incorporating the calibrated noise model and a noise-unaware estimator based on the ideal Born measurement model, deriving unified non-asymptotic sample complexity guarantees for each.
AI.result: For the noise-aware estimator, the paper derives unified trace-norm recovery guarantees explicitly characterizing sample complexity dependence on three quantities: structured state-class complexity, measurement-ensemble complexity, and state preparation and measurement noise levels. For the noise-unaware estimator, it establishes a unified non-asymptotic recovery guarantee consisting of a statistical error term plus an additional deterministic bias term arising from model mismatch between the assumed ideal reconstruction model and the actual noisy observation process.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a general, unified theoretical treatment of noisy structured QST sample complexity, offering guarantees that cover diverse quantum state classes and both noise-model-aware and noise-model-unaware estimators, thereby giving a principled basis for designing efficient QST protocols under realistic noise conditions.

title: Quantum information loss
summary: We introduce a measure of information loss for any quantum process that may be modeled by a prepare-evolve-measure scenario: Alice prepares an ensemble of states that gets sent via a quantum channel to Bob, who then measures the output. As a quantum channel models open system dynamics, our measure of information loss quantifies Bob's inability to retrodict with certainty which state Alice sent through the channel. By minimizing this measure over all possible pure state ensemble decompositions of a fixed state $ρ$, and over all POVMs on the output of a channel $\mathcal{E}$, we arrive at an intrinsic notion of information loss for any state-channel pair $(ρ,\mathcal{E})$. We show that the vanishing of information loss with respect to all states supported on a fixed codespace $\mathcal{H}_{\text{code}}$ is equivalent to a condition we term \emph{universal pristineness}, which ensures that orthogonal pure states in $\mathcal{H}_{\text{code}}$ get sent via the channel $\mathcal{E}$ to possibly mixed states whose supports are orthogonal. Moreover, we prove universal pristineness is equivalent to the Knill-Laflamme conditions in quantum error correction, which are necessary and sufficient for the existence of a perfect recovery channel for all states supported on $\mathcal{H}_{\text{code}}$. As an application, we apply our framework to the Hayden-Preskill model of black hole evaporation, demonstrating that the evaporation channel becomes asymptotically universally pristine, thereby providing a purely channel-theoretic formulation of Page-time information retrieval.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces an information loss measure for quantum processes in prepare-evolve-measure scenarios, quantifying Bob's inability to retrodict Alice's input state. Minimizing over state ensembles and POVMs yields an intrinsic information loss for any state-channel pair. Vanishing of this loss on a codespace is equivalent to "universal pristineness," which is shown to be equivalent to the Knill-Laflamme conditions of quantum error correction. The framework is applied to the Hayden-Preskill black hole evaporation model, providing a channel-theoretic formulation of Page-time information retrieval.
AI.motivation: To develop a rigorous, operational measure of information loss for quantum processes within the prepare-evolve-measure paradigm, and to connect this measure to fundamental conditions in quantum error correction and black hole information theory.
AI.method: Define an information-loss measure based on Bob's retrodiction uncertainty in a prepare-evolve-measure scenario, minimize it over pure-state ensemble decompositions of a fixed state and over POVMs on the channel output, and characterize when this minimized loss vanishes via a condition termed "universal pristineness." Prove equivalence between universal pristineness and the Knill-Laflamme conditions, then apply the framework to the Hayden-Preskill evaporation model.
AI.result: The vanishing of information loss for all states on a codespace is equivalent to universal pristineness (orthogonal code states map to states with orthogonal supports). Universal pristineness is proven equivalent to the Knill-Laflamme conditions for quantum error correction. The Hayden-Preskill evaporation channel is shown to become asymptotically universally pristine, yielding a channel-theoretic description of Page-time information retrieval.
AI.conclusion: The proposed information-loss measure unifies retrodiction-based information quantification with quantum error correction and black hole physics, showing that perfect recoverability (Knill-Laflamme), pristine channel behavior, and Page-time information retrieval all share the same underlying structural condition.
