title: How Much Reconstruction Does Quantum Machine Learning Need? Late Fusion of Independently Trained Quantum Subcircuits
summary: Circuit cutting lets a large quantum neural network (QNN) run as independent subcircuits on small devices, but rebuilding its outputs by reconstruction carries a classical sampling overhead exponential in the number of cuts - the dominant runtime cost in prior work. We ask whether, for machine-learning tasks, this step is necessary, and replace it with late fusion: each subcircuit is trained and measured independently, and a small classical head combines their outputs - a linear-cost, decision-level combination borrowed from multimodal learning. To characterize the trade-off we introduce a quantumness dial $Q$, a tunable reconstruction budget interpolating from pure fusion to full reconstruction, and a cut-entanglement diagnostic that indicates how much reconstruction a task needs (Spearman $ρ=0.59$ over $104$ runs). Across synthetic and standard datasets, independently trained late fusion matches full reconstruction accuracy within $0.04$ at every point of the controlled sweep and on every classical benchmark, at exponentially lower cost; it is also markedly more robust to shot and device noise. Controlled entangled-data experiments locate the boundary where fusion must fail. We do not claim advantage over classical machine learning - consistent with recent benchmarking, quantum offers no accuracy edge on these datasets. Late fusion is thus an efficient, noise-robust, self-characterizing alternative to reconstruction for circuit-cutting QML.

AI.tldr: Circuit cutting for quantum neural networks typically requires exponentially costly reconstruction to combine subcircuit outputs. The authors replace this with "late fusion"—a linear-cost, decision-level combination from multimodal learning—and show it matches full reconstruction accuracy within 0.04 at exponentially lower cost, while being more noise-robust. They introduce a quantumness dial Q and a cut-entanglement diagnostic (Spearman ρ=0.59) to locate tasks where fusion suffices versus where reconstruction is needed.
AI.motivation: Rebuilding outputs after circuit cutting carries a classical sampling overhead exponential in the number of cuts, which is the dominant runtime cost in prior work. The authors ask whether this reconstruction step is even necessary for machine-learning tasks, motivating a cheaper alternative.
AI.method: Replace reconstruction with late fusion: each subcircuit is trained and measured independently, and a small classical head combines outputs. Introduce a quantumness dial Q (tunable reconstruction budget from pure fusion to full reconstruction) and a cut-entanglement diagnostic to indicate how much reconstruction a task needs. Validate on synthetic and standard datasets, with controlled entangled-data experiments.
AI.result: Independently trained late fusion matches full reconstruction accuracy within 0.04 at every controlled sweep point and on every classical benchmark, at exponentially lower cost, and is markedly more robust to shot and device noise. The cut-entanglement diagnostic correlates with reconstruction need (Spearman ρ=0.59 over 104 runs). No quantum accuracy advantage over classical ML is claimed.
AI.conclusion: Late fusion is an efficient, noise-robust, self-characterizing alternative to reconstruction for circuit-cutting QML, with the diagnostic helping locate the boundary where fusion must fail.

title: Provably Efficient Self-Calibrating Quantum Fault Tolerance
summary: Quantum error correction protects logical information only when every physical operation remains below the fault-tolerance threshold, a condition that must be maintained continuously rather than only at the initial calibration. In practice, however, analog control parameters inevitably drift because of environmental fluctuations. As future fault-tolerant quantum computations are expected to run for days or even months, interrupting computation for repeated recalibration becomes fundamentally impractical. A promising alternative is to integrate calibration directly into computation by repurposing syndrome measurements as a calibration signal (Sivak et al, Nature 2026), but whether such self-calibration can be achieved with provable efficiency remains an open question. Here we establish a theoretical framework for self-calibrating quantum fault tolerance. We prove that, for a broad class of control-induced errors, the detection rate defines a locally strongly convex surrogate objective for analog calibration with high probability. This geometric property enables efficient online optimization using only syndrome measurements collected during normal error correction. We prove convergence to an $\varepsilon$ detection rate within $O(1/\varepsilon^2)$ epochs for time-independent drifts and also establish guarantees for time-dependent drifts. We further show that the convergence rate is independent of the code distance for quantum low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes. Pulse-level simulations of neutral-atom arrays and large-scale circuit-level Clifford simulations confirm these theoretical predictions. Our results establish self-calibrating fault tolerance as a provably efficient paradigm in which the same syndrome measurements simultaneously protect logical information and stabilize the underlying hardware.

AI.tldr: This paper establishes a theoretical framework for self-calibrating quantum fault tolerance, proving that syndrome measurements can be repurposed as calibration signals to correct control parameter drift during computation. The authors prove convergence guarantees for online optimization of analog control parameters using only syndrome data, with rates independent of code distance for quantum LDPC codes, and verify their results with neutral-atom and circuit-level simulations.
AI.motivation: Quantum error correction requires all physical operations to remain below the fault-tolerance threshold at all times, but analog control parameters inevitably drift due to environmental fluctuations. Since future fault-tolerant quantum computations are expected to run for days or months, interrupting computation for repeated recalibration is impractical. The authors seek a provably efficient way to integrate calibration directly into computation using syndrome measurements as the calibration signal.
AI.method: The authors prove that for a broad class of control-induced errors, the detection rate defines a locally strongly convex surrogate objective for analog calibration with high probability. This geometric property enables efficient online optimization using only syndrome measurements collected during normal error correction. They prove convergence to an ε detection rate in O(1/ε²) epochs for time-independent drifts and establish guarantees for time-dependent drifts, and show the convergence rate is independent of code distance for quantum LDPC codes.
AI.result: The theoretical convergence guarantees are confirmed by pulse-level simulations of neutral-atom arrays and large-scale circuit-level Clifford simulations. The results demonstrate that self-calibrating fault tolerance is a provably efficient paradigm where syndrome measurements simultaneously protect logical information and stabilize underlying hardware.
AI.conclusion: Self-calibration via syndrome-based online optimization is provably efficient for fault-tolerant quantum computation, achieving convergence rates independent of code distance for LDPC codes, thereby eliminating the need for disruptive in-situ recalibration during long-running computations.

title: Beyond transversality: structure of Clifford circuits for CSS codes
summary:
We characterize four groups of Clifford circuits for Calderbank--Shor--Steane (CSS) codes that are relevant to fault-tolerant logical operations. First, we show that every code-preserving Clifford circuit is a product of Z-diagonal circuits, composed of S and CZ gates, and their X-basis analogues. Second, we define the two-fold transversal group, generated by depth-one two-local code-preserving circuits, and show that each of its elements can be expressed as a product of layers consisting of either Z-diagonal, X-diagonal, or CNOT gates. As a corollary, every transversal gate is a product of three transversal diagonal circuits; for connected non-self-dual codes, two such circuits suffice.
  We further show that every code-preserving automorphism circuit, consisting of single-qubit Clifford gates and permutations, has a normal form comprising a Hadamard layer, a permutation, and two diagonal circuits. We also define a two-fold automorphism group, in which a depth-one two-local circuit may be code-preserving up to a permutation, and show that its logical image can be larger than that of the two-fold transversal group.
  For 136 CSS codes, we provide explicit generators and determine the logical image of the two-fold transversal group. We find 78 codes whose full logical Clifford group is generated by two-fold-transversal circuits, including codes of distances 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, and 12, with respective rates $2/5$, $3/4$, $1/9$, $1/5$, $2/5$, and $3/56$. We construct three families of CSS codes from bipartite grids, cut-complements, and quadrics, many of which realize the full logical Clifford group in this way. More generally, the induced logical group can be large even when it is not full logical Clifford group: it has order at least $460\,800$ for the gross code and roughly $10^{26}$ for a clustered-cyclic code.

AI.tldr: The paper characterizes four groups of Clifford circuits for CSS codes relevant to fault-tolerant logical operations, showing decompositions into diagonal circuits and CNOT layers, providing normal forms for automorphism circuits, and identifying 78 codes where the full logical Clifford group is generated by two-fold-transversal circuits.
AI.motivation: Understanding which logical operations can be implemented fault-tolerantly on quantum error-correcting codes is central to fault-tolerant quantum computation. Characterizing the structure of code-preserving Clifford circuits helps determine what transversal and other low-overhead logical gates are achievable for CSS codes.
AI.method: The authors define and study four groups of Clifford circuits for CSS codes: code-preserving Cliffords, the two-fold transversal group, automorphism circuits, and the two-fold automorphism group. They prove decomposition theorems (e.g., every code-preserving Clifford circuit is a product of Z- and X-diagonal circuits; every transversal gate is a product of up to three transversal diagonal circuits), provide normal forms, and perform a systematic analysis over 136 CSS codes with explicit generator constructions.
AI.result: They prove structural decomposition results for Clifford circuit groups, show that two-fold transversal circuits generate the full logical Clifford group for 78 codes (with distances 3-12 and various rates), and construct three families of CSS codes realizing full logical Clifford group via two-fold-transversal circuits. Even when not full, induced logical groups can be very large (e.g., order ~5e5 for the gross code and ~1e26 for a clustered-cyclic code).
AI.conclusion: Two-fold transversal circuits provide a powerful and general mechanism for generating logical Clifford operations on CSS codes, with many codes admitting the full logical Clifford group from these low-depth circuits. The structural characterizations offer a framework for designing fault-tolerant logical gate sets.

title: Improved regret bounds for structured online learning of quantum states
summary:
Quantum state tomography is fundamental to quantum information processing but becomes infeasible at scale due to the exponential growth of the state space. Shadow tomography alleviates this challenge by focusing on predicting measurement outcomes rather than reconstructing the full state. Its online variant models adaptive and potentially adversarial measurement scenarios, where a learner sequentially predicts outcomes while competing with the best fixed quantum state in hindsight.
  We show that exploiting additional structure in the measurements leads to significantly stronger regret guarantees. In particular, under the assumption that the adversarial measurements have bounded Frobenius norm, we analyze Projected Online Gradient Descent and derive regret bounds that depend on intrinsic structural properties, such as rank or sparsity, rather than the ambient Hilbert space dimension. As a complementary result, we show that one can achieve logarithmic regret, independent of both the number of qubits and measurement outcomes, for multi-outcome measurements under squared $L_2$ loss. These results demonstrate that incorporating realistic structural assumptions can substantially enhance the learnability of quantum states in online environments.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes online quantum state tomography with adversarial measurements, showing that exploiting structural properties (bounded Frobenius norm, rank, sparsity) of measurements leads to significantly stronger regret guarantees. Projected Online Gradient Descent achieves regret bounds depending on intrinsic structure rather than ambient Hilbert space dimension, and logarithmic regret is achievable for multi-outcome measurements under squared L2 loss.
AI.motivation: Quantum state tomography is infeasible at scale due to exponential growth of state space. While shadow tomography and its online variant address this challenge, existing regret guarantees depend on the ambient Hilbert space dimension, which is exponential in the number of qubits. The authors aim to show that exploiting realistic structural assumptions about measurements can yield dramatically stronger guarantees.
AI.method: The paper analyzes Projected Online Gradient Descent (POGD) for online shadow tomography with adversarial measurements. Under the assumption that adversarial measurements have bounded Frobenius norm, it derives regret bounds that depend on intrinsic structural properties such as rank or sparsity. It also analyzes multi-outcome measurements under squared L2 loss to achieve logarithmic regret.
AI.result: Two key results: (1) Under bounded Frobenius norm assumptions on adversarial measurements, Projected Online Gradient Descent achieves regret bounds depending on intrinsic structural properties (e.g., rank, sparsity) rather than the ambient Hilbert space dimension. (2) For multi-outcome measurements under squared L2 loss, logarithmic regret is achievable, independent of both the number of qubits and measurement outcomes.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating realistic structural assumptions about measurements substantially enhances the learnability of quantum states in online environments, demonstrating that the intrinsic complexity of the problem is much lower than the ambient dimension suggests.

title: Finite Quantum Histories: Holonomy Spectra, Minimal Clocks, and Exact Clock-Change Covariance
comment: 10 pages, 1 figure; independent finite-matrix verification code included
summary: We solve cyclic finite-dimensional quantum histories for arbitrary time-dependent unitary steps, without assuming that one step has finite order. The propagation Hamiltonian is a unitary connection Laplacian on a cycle; its complete gauge invariant is the monodromy $M=U_{L-1}\cdots U_0$. Its spectrum is $λ_{a,k}=1-\cos((2πk-θ_a)/L)$, where $e^{iθ_a}\in\mathrm{spec}(M)$. Thus the exact history sector is isomorphic to $\mathrm{Fix}(M)$, while frustration, the gap above a nonempty zero-energy sector, the determinant, and the finite-temperature trace are obtained in closed form. Ordinary spectral data recover the multiset of monodromy phase cosines but not phase orientation; low energy certifies proximity to an exact relational history. We then define the predictive quotient of a sharp finite clock relative to an accessible operator system as the unique coarsest event alphabet preserving all conditional statistics on a history sector. A finite-error theorem shows that threshold clustering recovers this quotient when the minimum diamond separation of inequivalent event channels exceeds four times the estimation error, and proves an optimal record-count bound. With full matrix access and homogeneous step $U$, the minimal number of clock events is the projective order of $U$. We distinguish the normalizer of the clock algebra from transformations preserving the coherent history code and classify oriented exact sharp clock changes by $U(r)\times\mathbb{Z}_L$ on a rank-$r$ history sector; without orientation the cyclic factor becomes dihedral. Reversible changes of full-information clock fibers are necessarily unitary, so irreversible coarse-graining is not exact clock covariance. Minimal realizations of a complete history Gram kernel are uniquely unitarily equivalent, with a finite-data Procrustes bound. Independent finite-matrix code verifies the main results.

AI.tldr: The paper solves cyclic finite-dimensional quantum histories for arbitrary time-dependent unitary steps without the finite-order assumption, showing the spectrum is determined by the monodromy M=U_{L-1}...U_0. It derives closed-form results for the exact history sector (isomorphic to Fix(M)), frustration, determinant, and finite-temperature trace. It then defines the predictive quotient of a sharp finite clock, proves a finite-error theorem for threshold clustering recovery with optimal record-count bounds, classifies exact sharp clock transformations, and establishes unique unitary equivalence of minimal history Gram kernel realizations with a Procrustes bound.
AI.motivation: To provide a complete gauge-invariant characterization of cyclic quantum histories for arbitrary (not necessarily finite-order) unitary steps, and to develop a rigorous framework for predictive coarse-graining of finite quantum clocks with provable recovery guarantees under measurement error.
AI.method: The propagation Hamiltonian is treated as a unitary connection Laplacian on a cycle, with monodromy as the complete gauge invariant. Spectral analysis yields eigenvalues λ_{a,k}=1−cos((2πk−θ_a)/L). The exact history sector is identified with Fix(M). A predictive quotient is defined as the unique coarsest event alphabet preserving all conditional statistics. Threshold clustering recovers this quotient under a diamond-distance condition. Procrustes analysis and projective-order arguments are used for minimal clock realizations and classification of clock transformations.
AI.result: Closed-form expressions for the spectrum, frustration, determinant, and finite-temperature trace in terms of monodromy. A finite-error theorem for predictive quotient recovery with a 4×error diamond separation threshold and optimal record-count bound. Identification of the minimal clock event count as the projective order of U. Classification of oriented exact sharp clock changes by U(r)×Z_L and unoriented by a dihedral extension. Unitary uniqueness of minimal history Gram kernel realizations with a Procrustes bound. Independent finite-matrix verification of all main results.
AI.conclusion: The monodromy fully determines the gauge-invariant spectral structure of cyclic quantum histories, enabling exact solutions. The predictive quotient framework provides a principled, provably correct method for clock coarse-graining under estimation error. Exact clock changes must be unitary, and minimal complete realizations are essentially unique, with numerical verification confirming the theoretical results.

title: The Locality Gap: A Thermodynamic Law for Objective Facts
comment: 12 pages, 6 figures, 42 cited references; source and reproducibility archive included
summary: Objective facts in quantum Darwinism are values recorded redundantly in many independently accessible fragments of the environment. Redundancy does not create additional logical information, so its thermodynamic meaning has remained unclear. We show that it creates an exact work asymmetry between controllers with different access architectures. For a record cloud $F$ and a partition $\mathcal{P}$ into blocks that cannot be jointly controlled, the reversible isothermal erasure penalty relative to a global controller is $k_{\mathrm{B}}T$ times the partition total correlation. If the source event $X$ is supplied as catalytic classical side information, subtracting the corresponding penalty gives the source-loss law $\mathcal{F}_{\mathcal{P}}^{T}=k_{\mathrm{B}}T\left[\sum_{B\in\mathcal{P}}I(X{:}F_B)-I(X{:}F)\right]$. We call this the thermodynamic factuality charge. It ranges from $-k_{\mathrm{B}}T H(X)$ for perfect secret sharing to $(|\mathcal{P}|-1)k_{\mathrm{B}}T H(X)$ for perfect broadcast objectivity. Its normalized form defines a thermodynamic record number between $0$ and $|\mathcal{P}|$. We derive Landauer--Darwin bounds, endpoint-rigidity certificates, exact growth and partition-refinement laws, spectrum-broadcast saturation, and closed formulas for noisy classical and quantum collision models. The theory does not modify quantum mechanics or posit objective collapse; it identifies the thermodynamic resource generated by redundant records under restricted control.

AI.tldr: This paper establishes a thermodynamic interpretation of quantum Darwinism by showing that redundancy in environmental records creates an exact work asymmetry between controllers with different access architectures. The reversible isothermal erasure penalty relative to a global controller equals k_B T times the partition total correlation, and the associated source-loss law defines a "thermodynamic factuality charge" that ranges from -k_B T H(X) for perfect secret sharing to (|P|-1)k_B T H(X) for perfect broadcast objectivity.
AI.motivation: While quantum Darwinism has long established that redundancy in environmental records underpins objective facts, the thermodynamic meaning of this redundancy has remained unclear since redundancy does not add logical information. The paper aims to fill this gap by identifying redundancy as a thermodynamic resource generated under restricted control architectures.
AI.method: The authors analyze record clouds F partitioned into blocks that cannot be jointly controlled, and derive the reversible isothermal erasure penalty difference between a local (partitioned) and global controller. They use partition total correlation, introduce catalytic classical side information for the source event X, and derive the source-loss law. They further derive Landauer-Darwin bounds, endpoint-rigidity certificates, growth and partition-refinement laws, spectrum-broadcast saturation, and closed formulas for noisy classical and quantum collision models.
AI.result: The erasure penalty relative to a global controller is k_B T times the partition total correlation. Subtracting the corresponding penalty when X is supplied as catalytic classical side information yields the source-loss law F_P^T = k_B T[Σ_B∈P I(X:F_B) - I(X:F)], termed the thermodynamic factuality charge. This charge ranges from -k_B T H(X) for perfect secret sharing to (|P|-1)k_B T H(X) for perfect broadcast objectivity, with a normalized form defining a thermodynamic record number between 0 and |P|.
AI.conclusion: Redundancy is not thermodynamically inert; it creates an exact work asymmetry between controllers with different access architectures. The theory does not modify quantum mechanics or posit objective collapse but identifies the thermodynamic resource generated by redundant records under restricted control.

title: Quantum One-Way Functions and Related Cryptographic Primitives
summary: Quantum cryptographic primitives beyond key distribution remain a less well understood area of research. In classical cryptography, one-way functions underpin nearly all standard cryptographic protocols, motivating the search for meaningful quantum analogues and for a clear understanding of the physical and computational mechanisms that could enforce one-wayness. In this article, we review quantum one-way functions and a range of closely related quantum-state primitives, including one-way state generators, pseudorandom quantum states, and efficiently indistinguishable pairs of states. We discuss both computational and information-theoretic notions of quantum one-wayness, emphasizing the different adversarial models and security assumptions that underlie these constructions. We compare and contrast the various proposed primitives, and clarify their conceptual relationships. Particular emphasis is placed on questions of physical realizability, experimental feasibility, and robustness to noise. Finally, we outline open problems and future directions toward the development of practical quantum cryptographic primitives beyond key distribution, and the emergence of a broader quantum-cryptographic ecosystem.

AI.tldr: This paper reviews quantum one-way functions and related quantum-state primitives (one-way state generators, pseudorandom quantum states, efficiently indistinguishable state pairs), comparing computational and information-theoretic notions of one-wayness, their adversarial models, physical realizability, and noise robustness, while outlining open problems for practical quantum cryptography beyond key distribution.
AI.motivation: Classical cryptography relies heavily on one-way functions as the foundation of nearly all standard protocols, but the quantum analogue remains underdeveloped. The authors seek to clarify the landscape of quantum one-way primitives to better understand the physical and computational mechanisms that could enforce one-wayness in the quantum setting, and to guide the development of practical quantum cryptographic protocols beyond key distribution.
AI.method: The paper is a review article that systematically surveys quantum one-way functions and closely related primitives, including one-way state generators, pseudorandom quantum states, and efficiently indistinguishable pairs of states. It analyzes both computational and information-theoretic notions of quantum one-wayness, compares distinct adversarial models and security assumptions, and clarifies conceptual relationships among the proposed primitives. Particular attention is given to physical realizability, experimental feasibility, and robustness to noise.
AI.result: The review provides a comprehensive comparison and contrast of various quantum one-way primitives, clarifying their conceptual relationships and differences in adversarial models and security assumptions. It highlights distinctions between computational and information-theoretic one-wayness and assesses the physical realizability and experimental feasibility of each construction.
AI.conclusion: The authors conclude by identifying open problems and future research directions toward developing practical quantum cryptographic primitives beyond key distribution, envisioning the emergence of a broader quantum-cryptographic ecosystem.

title: Multi-cavity strong coupling to an electron spin ensemble: spectral and dark-state signatures
summary: Spin ensembles are considered as potential candidates for quantum memory and quantum enhanced sensing applications. Here, we explore the controlled coupling of multiple superconducting microwave cavities to a spin ensemble, which shows signatures of strong coupling and, due to the multi-mode character, the formation of dark states. In particular, the latter are of interest, as they provide a potential pathway to enhance memory times and enable protected storage of non-classical states in spin ensembles due to the suppressed coupling to the circuit environment. We model the spin multi-cavity hybrid to reproduce the spectra and extract characteristic coupling strengths using the input-output formalism.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates hybrid systems coupling multiple superconducting microwave cavities to a spin ensemble, demonstrating strong coupling and the formation of dark states that could enable enhanced quantum memory times and protected storage of non-classical states.
AI.motivation: Spin ensembles are promising for quantum memory and quantum-enhanced sensing, but their coupling to circuit environments limits performance. Exploring multi-mode cavity coupling and dark states offers a pathway to suppress decoherence and extend memory times.
AI.method: The authors experimentally explore the controlled coupling of multiple superconducting microwave cavities to a spin ensemble. They model the spin multi-cavity hybrid system using the input-output formalism to reproduce the observed spectra and extract characteristic coupling strengths.
AI.result: Signatures of strong coupling are observed between the multiple cavities and the spin ensemble. The multi-mode character reveals the formation of dark states characterized by suppressed coupling to the circuit environment.
AI.conclusion: Dark states formed in the spin multi-cavity hybrid system provide a potential pathway for enhanced quantum memory times and protected storage of non-classical states in spin ensembles.

title: QSCI-CMP: Quantum-Selected Configuration Interaction with Chemically Motivated Preselection
summary: We present QSCI-CMP, a quantum-classical hybrid algorithm for molecular ground-state calculations that reduces both the query count and the gate count of sample-based quantum diagonalization with amplitude amplification (SQD-AA). SQD-AA mitigates the measurement bottleneck of quantum-selected configuration interaction (QSCI) by amplifying the basis states that have not yet been measured. Its oracle, however, specifies the measured states by listing them one by one, so its gate count grows with the number of collected states. Moreover, the quantum resources are spent even on states whose importance is evident from chemical knowledge, such as low-order excitations from the Hartree-Fock reference, which could be collected classically at the outset. We therefore propose to fix such chemically trivial states in advance, include them in the diagonalization subspace from the start, and exclude them from the amplification target, using a low-cost oracle that recognizes them through the excitation level and the seniority number of each basis state. We numerically demonstrate that QSCI-CMP reduces the query count and the gate count required to reach chemical accuracy by up to approximately 68% and 72% relative to SQD-AA for 24-qubit systems. The chemically trivial subspace is freely tunable within the classical computational budget. A larger subspace shifts more work onto the classical solver and increases the reduction in quantum cost, and when it captures the ground state sufficiently well, no quantum sampling is needed at all. We also point out that a query-optimal iteration count known from the analysis of quantum search further reduces the query count of both methods by approximately 12%.

AI.tldr: QSCI-CMP is a quantum-classical hybrid algorithm for molecular ground-state calculations that pre-fixes chemically trivial basis states (identified by excitation level and seniority number) into the diagonalization subspace classically, excluding them from the quantum amplification target. This reduces query count and gate count by up to ~68% and ~72% respectively compared to SQD-AA for 24-qubit systems, and a query-optimal iteration count further reduces queries by ~12% for both methods.
AI.motivation: SQD-AA mitigates the measurement bottleneck of QSCI but has two drawbacks: its oracle's gate count grows with the number of collected states, and quantum resources are wasted amplifying states (e.g., low-order excitations from the Hartree-Fock reference) whose importance is already known from chemical intuition and could be collected classically. The authors aim to eliminate this waste by handling such chemically trivial states without quantum resources.
AI.method: The algorithm pre-selects chemically trivial states (identified via excitation level and seniority number) and includes them in the diagonalization subspace from the start, excluding them from the amplification target. A low-cost oracle recognizes these states through excitation level and seniority number. The chemically trivial subspace is tunable within classical computational budget. Additionally, a query-optimal iteration count from quantum search analysis is applied.
AI.result: Numerical demonstrations on 24-qubit systems show QSCI-CMP reduces query count and gate count by up to approximately 68% and 72% relative to SQD-AA. A larger chemically trivial subspace shifts more work to the classical solver and increases quantum cost reduction. When the subspace captures the ground state sufficiently well, no quantum sampling is needed. The query-optimal iteration count reduces query count of both methods by approximately 12%.
AI.conclusion: QSCI-CMP effectively minimizes quantum resource expenditure by classically handling chemically obvious basis states, offering significant improvements in both query and gate counts. The approach provides a tunable trade-off between classical and quantum computational cost, and can eliminate quantum sampling entirely when the classical subspace is sufficient.

title: Robust logarithmic lower bound on shared-resource cost for $f$-routing
summary: In one-round $f$-routing, Alice receives an $n$-bit string and an unknown qubit, while Bob receives another $n$-bit string. They exchange one simultaneous message each, and the value of $f$ determines which party must recover the qubit. Message lengths, local systems, and local operations are unrestricted. We charge only $E_{\dim}(ρ_{LR})=\log_2\min\{\operatorname{rank}ρ_L,\operatorname{rank}ρ_R\}$, the logarithm of the smaller marginal support dimension of the shared state prepared before the inputs arrive. The state may be arbitrary and mixed. For the inner product modulo $2$, we prove that every protocol with worst-case error at most $0.09$ in both routing cases, measured in the full, unhalved diamond norm, satisfies $d\log_2(2d)=Ω(n)$ for $d=\min\{\operatorname{rank}ρ_L,\operatorname{rank}ρ_R\}$. Thus $d=Ω(n/\log n)$ and $E_{\dim}(ρ_{LR})\ge\log_2 n-\log_2\log_2 n-O(1)$. The closest earlier growing Schmidt-rank lower bound for an explicit routing function assumes zero error in one routing case. Our proof converts correctness into a matrix whose entries have a constant gap between the two routing cases. It approximates this matrix by one whose rank depends on $d$, but not on the dimensions of messages or local systems. A sign-rank lower bound for the matrix of the inner product modulo $2$ completes the argument. A lower bound polynomial in $n$ on $E_{\dim}$ remains open.

AI.tldr: This paper studies one-round quantum f-routing protocols, proving that for the inner product modulo 2 function, any protocol achieving worst-case error at most 0.09 in both routing cases requires the prepared shared state to have marginal support dimension d satisfying d·log₂(2d) = Ω(n). This implies E_dim ≥ log₂ n − log₂ log₂ n − O(1), improving upon the previously closest bound which only assumed zero error in one routing case. The proof converts protocol correctness into a matrix with a constant gap between routing cases, approximates it by a rank-bounded matrix, and completes the argument using a sign-rank lower bound.
AI.motivation: To establish lower bounds on communication complexity for quantum routing tasks in terms of the entanglement dimension of the pre-shared state, specifically improving upon existing Schmidt-rank lower bounds that only held under stricter zero-error assumptions and single routing case conditions.
AI.method: The proof constructs a matrix whose entries encode a constant gap between the two routing cases. This matrix is then approximated by another matrix whose rank is bounded in terms of d (the smaller marginal support dimension) but independent of message or local system dimensions. A sign-rank lower bound for the inner product modulo 2 matrix is applied to complete the argument.
AI.result: Every protocol with worst-case error ≤ 0.09 in both routing cases satisfies d·log₂(2d) = Ω(n), where d is the minimum marginal rank. Consequently, d = Ω(n/log n) and E_dim(ρ_LR) ≥ log₂ n − log₂ log₂ n − O(1). This improves the earlier bound that required zero error in one routing case.
AI.conclusion: The paper establishes a growing lower bound on the entanglement dimension for explicit routing functions under constant error in both routing cases, closing some gap from prior zero-error results. It leaves open the question of whether a polynomial lower bound on E_dim in n can be achieved.

title: Symmetry-guided construction and exact certification of absolutely maximally entangled states
comment: 15 pages, 8 figures. Results were found and written up with the help of Claude Fable 5 (Anthropic) and ChatGPT 5.6 Sol (OpenAI). AME(12,5) was found within 3 hours of beginning the investigation, with the other 4 AME states found autonomously while preparing the manuscript
summary: We construct Hermitian self-dual maximum-distance-separable codes with parameters $[12,6,7]_{25}$, $[18,9,10]_{121}$, and $[18,9,10]_{169}$. Through the nonbinary stabilizer construction these codes define $\text{AME}(12,5)$, $\text{AME}(18,11)$, and $AMD(18,13)$ states, and one-party projection gives $\text{AME}(17,11)$ and $\text{AME}(17,13)$. The $[12,6,7]_{25}$ code, which is not monomially equivalent to a generalized Reed-Solomon code, is obtained by a systematic search without prescribed coordinate symmetry; its monomial-semilinear automorphism group acts with a regular $\mathbb{Z}_3^2$ orbit on nine coordinates. Imposing that action on two nine-coordinate orbits reduces the length-eighteen search to a nine-element group algebra kernel, whose Hermitian character decomposition splits the invariant self-duality constraints into independent blocks with exact family counts; a norm-one coordinate scaling removes a factor $q+1=14$ at $q=13$. Hermitian self-duality and the MDS property are certified by exact field arithmetic and complete square-minor enumeration. Graph-state cut-rank computations, including all single-vertex deletions of the length-eighteen graphs, provide additional exact checks.

AI.tldr: The paper constructs three new Hermitian self-dual maximum-distance-separable codes with parameters [12,6,7]_{25}, [18,9,10]_{121}, and [18,9,10]_{169}, which via the nonbinary stabilizer construction yield absolutely maximally entangled (AME) states of various dimensions, including AME(12,5), AME(18,11), AME(18,13), AME(17,11), and AME(17,13). The constructions involve systematic search, group-symmetry-based reduction to a group algebra kernel, and exact certification by field arithmetic and complete minor enumeration.
AI.motivation: To construct new Hermitian self-dual MDS codes that generate absolutely maximally entangled quantum states, particularly addressing parameter regimes not covered by existing generalized Reed-Solomon codes.
AI.method: Systematic search for the [12,6,7]_{25} code without prescribed coordinate symmetry; use of the monomial-semilinear automorphism group with a regular Z_3^2 orbit on nine coordinates; reduction of the length-eighteen search to a nine-element group algebra kernel via group-symmetry imposition; Hermitian character decomposition to split invariant self-duality constraints into independent blocks; norm-one coordinate scaling to remove a factor q+1=14 at q=13; exact field arithmetic and complete square-minor enumeration for certification; graph-state cut-rank computations including all single-vertex deletions.
AI.result: Three new Hermitian self-dual MDS codes constructed; they define AME(12,5), AME(18,11), and AME(18,13) states via nonbinary stabilizer construction; one-party projection yields AME(17,11) and AME(17,13); the [12,6,7]_{25} code is not monomially equivalent to any generalized Reed-Solomon code, representing a genuinely new family; exact counts of families obtained from the character decomposition.
AI.conclusion: The paper demonstrates a powerful combination of group-theoretic symmetry reduction and exact algebraic computation to construct new Hermitian self-dual MDS codes and associated AME states, achieving previously unknown parameter values.

title: Quantum error correction with global control
summary: Reaching fault tolerance means scaling qubit counts by orders of magnitude, a jump that conventional superconducting architectures cannot sustain without solving the so-called `wiring problem'. Global control sidesteps this bottleneck, but implementing quantum error correction (QEC) on previously proposed global architectures incurs extremely steep overhead costs, due to the need for separate correction procedures for the computational and auxiliary qubits that comprise the global device. We resolve this by introducing the first globally-controlled architecture with zero qubit overhead. Every physical qubit is a computational qubit, and thus, every qubit is protected under a single error correcting scheme. We identify a class of cyclic stabilizer codes realizable through global iSWAP and single-qubit gates, yielding QEC thresholds nearly seven orders of magnitude larger than previous estimates for globally-controlled arrays. We further show these thresholds improve systematically as the global architecture is augmented with a limited amount of local measurement sites, demonstrating a trade-off between wiring simplicity and fault-tolerant performance.

AI.tldr: Introduces the first globally-controlled quantum computing architecture with zero qubit overhead, where every physical qubit doubles as a computational qubit, protected by a single cyclic stabilizer code implemented via global iSWAP and single-qubit gates, achieving QEC thresholds nearly seven orders of magnitude higher than prior global-control estimates.
AI.motivation: Conventional superconducting quantum architectures face a "wiring problem" when scaling to fault tolerance, while previously proposed globally-controlled architectures suffer from steep qubit overhead because they require separate error correction procedures for computational and auxiliary qubits.
AI.method: The authors design a globally-controlled architecture where all physical qubits are computational qubits, eliminating qubit overhead entirely. They identify a class of cyclic stabilizer codes realizable through global iSWAP and single-qubit gates, and analyze performance with varying local measurement site augmentation.
AI.result: The proposed architecture achieves QEC thresholds nearly seven orders of magnitude larger than previous estimates for globally-controlled arrays. Thresholds improve systematically when the architecture is augmented with a limited number of local measurement sites, establishing a trade-off between wiring simplicity and fault-tolerant performance.
AI.conclusion: Global control with cyclic stabilizer codes can provide a viable path to fault tolerance without a wiring bottleneck, and augmenting the architecture with modest local measurement capability yields further performance gains.

title: Exponential Speedup of Entanglement Generation by Quantum Mpemba Effects
summary: Entanglement is a key resource for quantum technologies. We show that protocols employing quantum Mpemba effects allow one to exponentially accelerate the generation of entanglement, or to slow down the decay thereof. Two entanglement Mpemba effects with different operational meaning are introduced, focusing either on the task of rapidly generating a certain threshold value for entanglement or on achieving the asymptotic steady-state value. We show that entanglement Mpemba effects depend on the chosen entanglement measure. Using cluster elimination methods, many-body quantum systems also benefit from the exponential speedup of entanglement generation, as we demonstrate for a dissipative long-range Ising chain.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates that quantum Mpemba effects can exponentially accelerate entanglement generation or slow its decay. Two types of entanglement Mpemba effects are introduced with different operational meanings, and the effects are shown to be measure-dependent. Using cluster elimination methods, the exponential speedup is demonstrated in dissipative long-range Ising chains.
AI.motivation: Entanglement is a key resource for quantum technologies, so finding ways to rapidly generate entanglement or prevent its decay is of fundamental importance. The Mpemba effect (where a hotter system cools faster than a colder one) is translated to quantum entanglement, offering a potential protocol-level advantage.
AI.method: The paper introduces two distinct entanglement Mpemba effects with different operational meanings: one targeting rapid generation of a threshold entanglement value, and another targeting the asymptotic steady-state value. The dependence of these effects on the chosen entanglement measure is analyzed. Cluster elimination methods are employed to extend the exponential acceleration to many-body quantum systems, specifically demonstrated on a dissipative long-range Ising chain.
AI.result: Protocols employing quantum Mpemba effects achieve exponential acceleration of entanglement generation or exponential slowdown of entanglement decay. The Mpemba effects are shown to depend on the choice of entanglement measure. The exponential speedup is successfully demonstrated in a many-body dissipative long-range Ising chain using cluster elimination methods.
AI.conclusion: Quantum Mpemba effects provide a powerful operational tool for controlling entanglement dynamics, enabling exponential speedups in entanglement generation for both few-body and many-body quantum systems, though the effects are measure-dependent.

title: Dynamical phase transition in generalized Dicke model with strongly interacting trapped Rydberg ions
summary: We study dynamical phase transitions in the generalized dissipative Dicke model in an array of trapped Rydberg ions, where their density-density interactions compete with the collective spin-phonon coupling, laser driving and dissipation. This setting offers a versatile approach to study equilibrium as well as non-equilibrium many-body phenomena, as parameters, such as the Ising interaction, laser-ion and spin-phonon coupling can be tuned. Through analyzing the mean-field phase diagram, we find a variety of distinct phases and the emergence of a tricritical point that are sensitively dependent of the interaction between Rydberg ions. We then study the quantum dynamics for a finite system size and characterize parameter dependent dynamics using the spin average, entropy, and Loschmidt echo. Distinctive signatures of the dynamical phases, such as slow relaxation and metastability, arise near the phase transition. This analysis predicts rich quantum dynamics of the finite system that link to the non-equilibrium mean-field phases. Our study widens the exploration of collective and non-equilibrium phases in Dicke models, and reveals that the Rydberg ion interaction drastically affects the phase diagram and dynamics.

AI.tldr: The paper studies dynamical phase transitions in a generalized dissipative Dicke model implemented in an array of trapped Rydberg ions, where density-density (Ising) interactions compete with collective spin-phonon coupling, laser driving, and dissipation. Mean-field analysis reveals a rich phase diagram with a tricritical point depending sensitively on Rydberg ion interactions, while finite-size quantum dynamics show distinctive signatures (slow relaxation, metastability) near phase transitions that connect to the non-equilibrium mean-field phases.
AI.motivation: To broaden the exploration of collective and non-equilibrium phases in Dicke models by introducing tunable Rydberg ion interactions, enabling study of both equilibrium and non-equilibrium many-body phenomena in a single versatile platform.
AI.method: The authors perform mean-field phase diagram analysis to identify distinct phases and a tricritical point, and study quantum dynamics for finite system sizes by characterizing parameter-dependent dynamics using the spin average, entropy, and Loschmidt echo.
AI.result: They find a variety of distinct phases and a tricritical point whose location is sensitively dependent on the Rydberg ion interaction strength. Finite-size quantum dynamics reveal distinctive signatures of dynamical phases, including slow relaxation and metastability near phase transitions, which are linked to the non-equilibrium mean-field phases.
AI.conclusion: The Rydberg ion interaction drastically affects both the phase diagram and quantum dynamics, widening the exploration of collective and non-equilibrium phases in Dicke-type models and predicting rich quantum dynamics in finite systems.

title: Field-Space Entanglement Dynamics Between Tunnel-Coupled Luttinger Liquids
summary: Entanglement dynamics depend not only on how a quantum system is partitioned, but critically on how interactions across that partition are structured. For a spatial bipartition of a locally interacting system, entanglement is generated near the boundary and then propagates into the bulk. By contrast, when two extended quantum fields are coupled locally along their entire length, the interaction crosses the field-space partition everywhere, and this generates correlations throughout the system. Here, we study the entanglement dynamics between two gapless one-dimensional quantum many-body systems described by Luttinger liquid theory. The systems are initially decoupled and prepared at zero or finite temperature, after which a time-dependent tunneling interaction is activated uniformly along their length. Within a Gaussian approximation, we derive general analytical expressions for the logarithmic negativity, mutual information, and Rényi entropies under arbitrary coupling protocols. At zero temperature, entanglement displays an early-time power-law growth whose exponent is fixed solely by the first non-null derivative of the tunneling protocol. Once the coupling saturates, we obtain exact long-time averages of the information-theoretic quantities and characterise how the correlations scale with temperature and the final coupling strength. We also analyse how mutual information and logarithmic negativity approach the adiabatic limit for a very slow protocol with respect to intrinsic system timescale. This work extends the study of entanglement dynamics in nonequilibrium field theory to field-space partitions and mixed initial states.

AI.tldr: The paper studies entanglement dynamics between two gapless 1D quantum many-body systems (Luttinger liquids) that are coupled locally along their entire length via a time-dependent tunneling interaction. Using a Gaussian approximation, the authors derive analytical expressions for logarithmic negativity, mutual information, and Rényi entropies under arbitrary coupling protocols, revealing universal early-time power-law growth and long-time saturation behavior.
AI.motivation: Entanglement dynamics in nonequilibrium quantum systems is largely understood for spatial partitions where entanglement is generated at boundaries and propagates inward. However, for field-space partitions where interactions cross the partition everywhere (e.g., two extended quantum fields coupled locally along their entire length), correlations are generated throughout the system simultaneously. This distinct regime of entanglement dynamics, especially for mixed states and finite temperature, has not been systematically explored.
AI.method: The authors model two gapless 1D systems as Luttinger liquids, initially decoupled, prepared at zero or finite temperature. A time-dependent tunneling interaction is switched on uniformly along the entire length. Within a Gaussian approximation, they derive general analytical expressions for logarithmic negativity, mutual information, and Rényi entropies valid for arbitrary coupling protocols.
AI.result: At zero temperature, entanglement exhibits early-time power-law growth with an exponent fixed solely by the first non-null derivative of the tunneling protocol. For saturated coupling, exact long-time averages of information-theoretic quantities are obtained, and the scaling of correlations with temperature and final coupling strength is characterized. The approach to the adiabatic limit for slow protocols relative to intrinsic timescales is also analyzed for mutual information and logarithmic negativity.
AI.conclusion: This work generalizes the study of entanglement dynamics in nonequilibrium field theory to field-space partitions and mixed initial states, providing a comprehensive analytical framework for entanglement generation when interactions span the entire partition rather than a boundary.

title: Geometry-Only CSL/DP Ratios and the Nonuniqueness of Decoherence Kernels
summary: We study idealized levitated protocols that create spatial superpositions of massive test particles. For each protocol, we compare the dimensionless contrast-loss exponent of mass-proportional continuous spontaneous localization (CSL) with the Diósi--Penrose (DP) self-energy exponent $E_Gτ/\hbar$. We first prove that the point-particle CSL separation kernel has an exact random-unitary realization: Gaussian momentum kicks arriving at Poisson-distributed times produce the same unconditional decay of spatial coherence, although a pure state conditioned on the complete kick record remains pure. The separation kernel alone therefore specifies an operational decoherence law, not the occurrence of objective collapse. We then show that the ratio of the CSL and DP exponents is independent of particle mass and interrogation time. In the point-particle model it depends only on branch separation and an effective distance; for the standard GRW reference parameters, its resolved-superposition crossover is $x_*\approx1.91\,\mathrm{nm}$. For rigid spherical bodies with an arbitrary normalized radial mass profile, total mass, overall density scale, and interrogation time again cancel, leaving a dimensionless geometry factor. The results distinguish three requirements for a decisive experiment: detectable absolute effects, a controlled comparison of CSL and DP scales, and observables capable of discriminating physically different dynamics that share the same ensemble decoherence kernel.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes idealized levitated superpositions of massive particles, proving that the point-particle CSL separation kernel has an exact random-unitary realization and that the ratio of CSL to DP contrast-loss exponents is independent of mass and interrogation time, depending only on geometric factors (with a crossover at ~1.91 nm for standard GRW parameters). It distinguishes three requirements for decisive experiments comparing CSL and DP collapse models.
AI.motivation: To rigorously compare two prominent objective collapse models—mass-proportional CSL and the Diósi–Penrose self-energy model—in the context of levitated spatial superpositions, and to identify what experimental conditions would allow a decisive distinction between them.
AI.method: Derives exact analytical results: (1) proves the point-particle CSL separation kernel admits an exact random-unitary realization via Gaussian momentum kicks at Poisson-distributed times; (2) computes the ratio of CSL decay exponent to DP self-energy exponent E_Gτ/ħ and shows it cancels mass and time dependencies; (3) generalizes to rigid spherical bodies with arbitrary normalized radial mass profiles to obtain a dimensionless geometry factor.
AI.result: The CSL vs DP exponent ratio is independent of mass and interrogation time. In the point-particle model it depends only on branch separation and effective distance, with a resolved-superposition crossover at x_* ≈ 1.91 nm for standard GRW parameters. For rigid spherical bodies, the ratio reduces to a dimensionless geometry factor. Additionally, the separation kernel alone specifies an operational decoherence law but does not imply objective collapse, since conditioned pure states remain pure.
AI.conclusion: A decisive experiment must satisfy three distinct requirements: detect absolute collapse effects, provide a controlled comparison of CSL and DP scales, and use observables that can discriminate between physically different dynamics that share the same ensemble decoherence kernel.

title: Towards fault-tolerance with universal phase-error-transparent gates for high-spin cat codes
summary: High-dimensional nuclear spins offer a hardware-efficient route to quantum error correction (QEC), with the spin cat code providing intrinsic robustness against phase errors -- the dominant noise channel in donor-in-silicon architectures. However, realizing the full potential of this encoding requires gate operations that preserve its error-correcting properties. In this work, we construct a universal logical gate set that is error-transparent (ET) to phase errors, and discuss its practical implementations and challenges. The ET gates ensure that phase errors occurring stochastically during gate operations are propagated in a systematically traceable manner and remain correctable in a subsequent QEC step. Among the universal gate set constructed, we identify the logical $X$ gate as the primary challenge and discuss potential realization schemes. In addition, to fully leverage the spin cat code's advantage over an unencoded qubit, multi-tone microwave driving of the logical $CZ$ gate is essential. Our simulations show that ET gates significantly outperform non-ET gates and may be necessary to surpass the break-even point. We further show how logical measurement and recovery can be constructed from ET operations, and explain why state-preparation cannot be made ET. In particular, ET measurement in the computational basis is realizable via spin parity measurement, and that error correction circuits constructed from ET operations achieve optimal error correction capacity. Our work charts a concrete path toward full fault-tolerant quantum computation with high-dimensional nuclear spin systems.

AI.tldr: This work constructs a universal error-transparent (ET) logical gate set for the high-dimensional nuclear spin cat code, demonstrating that ET gates outperform non-ET gates and may be necessary to surpass break-even in fault-tolerant quantum computation using donor-in-silicon architectures.
AI.motivation: High-dimensional nuclear spins offer a hardware-efficient route to quantum error correction via the spin cat code, which provides intrinsic robustness against phase errors—the dominant noise channel in donor-in-silicon architectures. However, realizing the full potential of this encoding requires gate operations that preserve its error-correcting properties.
AI.method: The authors construct a universal logical gate set that is error-transparent to phase errors, analyze practical implementations and challenges, and identify the logical X gate as the primary challenge. They propose multi-tone microwave driving for the logical CZ gate and construct logical measurement and recovery from ET operations via spin parity measurement.
AI.result: Simulations show that ET gates significantly outperform non-ET gates and may be necessary to surpass the break-even point. Error correction circuits constructed from ET operations achieve optimal error correction capacity. ET measurement in the computational basis is realizable via spin parity measurement, though state preparation cannot be made ET.
AI.conclusion: The work charts a concrete path toward full fault-tolerant quantum computation with high-dimensional nuclear spin systems, highlighting the necessity of error-transparent operations for practical QEC.

title: A quantum framework for event graphs
comment: 7 pages, 2 figures, to be submitted to Physical Review Research
summary: Graph representations of discrete events provide a natural foundation for machine-learning models of anomaly detection, yet they also suggest a deeper quantum description in which graph structure gives rise to interacting quantum degrees of freedom. We develop a quantum framework based on a directed participant graph whose edges represent events connecting pairs of source and destination vertices. A line-graph transformation maps each event to a node of a bidirectional event graph, whose edges inherit relational information from the participant graph. Since event datasets are naturally organized as collections of event records, their raw attributes align directly with the nodes of the event graph. A quantum harmonic oscillator (QHO) is assigned to every node of the participant graph, with the collective Hilbert space of these QHOs providing a complete basis for representing quantum states. Every directed edge of the participant graph thereby acquires a Schwinger isospin arising from the two endpoint oscillators. Under the line-graph transformation, event-graph nodes correspond to observable isospins whose interactions through bidirectional edges provide a natural substrate for learning from event datasets, while the quantum states associated with the underlying participant nodes remain latent and inaccessible to direct observation. Within this framework we formulate a compact U(1) lattice gauge theory (LGT) on the event graph that leads to a Kogut-Susskind Hamiltonian (KSH) in the form of an XY-type spin model governing the dynamics of sparse anomalous-event isospins immersed in a bath of many nominal events. The proposed framework establishes a mathematical foundation for quantum-inspired graph-based anomaly detection and provides a principled bridge between graph learning, LGT, and quantum information.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a quantum-inspired framework for anomaly detection in event datasets using directed participant graphs, a line-graph transformation to event graphs, quantum harmonic oscillators assigned to nodes, Schwinger isospins on edges, and a U(1) lattice gauge theory formulated as a Kogut-Susskind Hamiltonian (XY-type spin model) to model sparse anomalous-event isospins in a bath of nominal events.
AI.motivation: Graph representations of discrete events are natural for machine-learning-based anomaly detection, but they also suggest a deeper quantum description where graph structure gives rise to interacting quantum degrees of freedom. The authors aim to establish a principled mathematical foundation bridging graph learning, lattice gauge theory, and quantum information for anomaly detection.
AI.method: A directed participant graph is constructed with edges representing events between source and destination vertices. A line-graph transformation maps each event to a node of a bidirectional event graph, whose edges inherit relational information. Each participant-graph node is assigned a quantum harmonic oscillator (QHO); the collective Hilbert space provides a basis for quantum states. Each directed edge acquires a Schwinger isospin from the two endpoint oscillators. Event-graph nodes correspond to observable isospins interacting via bidirectional edges, while participant-node quantum states remain latent. A compact U(1) lattice gauge theory is formulated on the event graph, yielding a Kogut-Susskind Hamiltonian in the form of an XY-type spin model.
AI.result: The proposed framework results in a Kogut-Susskind Hamiltonian expressed as an XY-type spin model that governs the dynamics of sparse anomalous-event isospins immersed in a bath of many nominal events, establishing a formal quantum description for graph-based anomaly detection.
AI.conclusion: The framework establishes a mathematical foundation for quantum-inspired graph-based anomaly detection and provides a principled bridge between graph learning, lattice gauge theory, and quantum information.

title: Balanced Routing for Symmetric Quantum Circuits
summary: Mapping quantum programs to restricted physical chips requires SWAP operations, incurring depth and error penalties. In symmetric programs, this routing overhead breaks theoretical symmetry because identical logical roles experience unequal shuffling. While often attributed to hardware topology alone, we show this is a two-level phenomenon. A qubit patch's shape dictates if it can host a balanced assignment. When balance is possible, the actual imbalance is set by the logical-to-physical assignment, meaning a balanced assignment can distribute routing costs perfectly evenly at no extra depth. Through exhaustive search on a 57-qubit "heavy-hex" lattice, we prove these topological constraints. For a four-part ring, 108 of 124 connected patches admit a cost-free balanced assignment, with the 16 exceptions being star-shaped. For a six-part ring, cost-free balance is impossible on compact patches. For a fully connected four-part symmetry, balance is structurally impossible at any depth. Simulations using realistic error rates show that, relative to the worst-case concentrated assignment, balanced assignments reduce symmetry-breaking by 92.7% (95% CI [+89.8%, +95.3%]) for the raw metric and 87.0% (95% CI [+79.6%, +94.1%]) for the decoherence-corrected measure (p = 2.45 x 10^-32). Substrate error heterogeneity accounts for at most 10.8% of this effect. Notably, switching to the compiler's highest generic optimization level did not yield a statistically significant change in routing imbalance, highlighting the need for targeted symmetry-aware passes. When patch geometry permits, routing imbalance is a compiler choice rather than a hardware limitation. Thus, symmetry-aware assignment should be a primary objective for compiler optimization and chip design.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that quantum circuit routing imbalance on restricted chips (e.g., heavy-hex lattices) is a two-level phenomenon—depending on both the qubit patch shape and the logical-to-physical assignment—not solely hardware topology. Balance is achievable at no extra depth when patch geometry permits (108 of 124 connected patches for a four-part ring), and balanced assignments reduce symmetry-breaking by up to 92.7%, revealing that symmetry-aware assignment should be a primary compiler and chip-design objective.
AI.motivation: When mapping symmetric quantum programs to physically restricted chips (e.g., heavy-hex lattices), SWAP-based routing breaks the theoretical symmetry of the program because identical logical roles undergo unequal shuffling. Historically, this was attributed solely to hardware topology. The authors aim to show this is a two-level problem—patch shape and logical-to-physical assignment—and that much of the imbalance is a compiler choice, not a hardware limitation.
AI.method: The authors systematically analyze the geometric/structural relationship between qubit patch shapes and the possibility of balanced (symmetry-preserving) logical-to-physical assignments. They perform exhaustive search over a 57-qubit heavy-hex lattice for four-part and six-part ring symmetries, as well as fully connected four-part symmetry, to classify which patch geometries admit cost-free balanced assignments. They then run simulations with realistic error rates comparing balanced versus worst-case concentrated assignments, measuring symmetry-breaking via a raw metric and a decoherence-corrected measure, with CI-based statistical analysis.
AI.result: For a four-part ring, 108 of 124 connected patches admit a cost-free balanced assignment; the 16 exceptions are star-shaped. For a six-part ring, cost-free balance is impossible on compact patches. For fully connected four-part symmetry, balance is structurally impossible at any depth. Balanced assignments reduce symmetry-breaking by 92.7% (95% CI [+89.8%, +95.3%]) on the raw metric and 87.0% (95% CI [+79.6%, +94.1%]) on the decoherence-corrected measure (p = 2.45 × 10^-32). Substrate error heterogeneity accounts for at most 10.8% of the effect. Switching to the compiler's highest optimization level produced no statistically significant change in routing imbalance.
AI.conclusion: Routing imbalance in symmetric quantum programs is not fundamentally a hardware limitation; when patch geometry permits it, it is a compiler choice. The authors argue that symmetry-aware assignment should be a primary optimization objective for both compiler design and chip architecture, since it can distribute routing costs perfectly evenly at no extra depth when the patch shape allows.

title: Time-Dependent Hamiltonian Simulation with Optimal Query Complexity

AI.tldr: A query-optimal algorithm for simulating general n-qubit time-dependent Hamiltonians, achieving O(αT + log(1/ε)/log(e + log(1/ε)/(αT))) HAM-T queries, matching the known lower bound for time-independent Hamiltonians and showing time dependence incurs no asymptotic overhead.
AI.motivation: Previous Hamiltonian simulation algorithms for time-dependent Hamiltonians did not match the query lower bounds achievable for time-independent cases. The authors aim to close this gap by constructing a query-optimal algorithm whose time dependence does not add asymptotic query overhead.
AI.method: The algorithm first builds a one-query transducer that, given an auxiliary state, approximates the time-ordered propagator U_H(T) while returning the auxiliary state unchanged. A weighted combination of circuits applying the transducer different numbers of times causes the error from omitting this state to decay factorially, yielding optimal precision dependence. For time-independent Hamiltonians, this also serves as a query-optimal alternative to qubitization.
AI.result: The algorithm achieves O(αT + log(1/ε)/log(e + log(1/ε)/(αT))) HAM-T queries for time-dependent Hamiltonian simulation, matching the known query lower bound for time-independent Hamiltonians.
AI.conclusion: Time-dependent Hamiltonian simulation can be performed with asymptotically no additional query overhead compared to the time-independent case, resolving the query complexity question for Lipschitz continuous Hamiltonians. The method also provides a new query-optimal approach for time-independent simulation, serving as an alternative to qubitization.

title: Hadamard sensing channel: deterministic artifact suppression for quantum sensors
summary: Dynamical decoupling sequences are essential for nanoscale quantum sensing, but the finite duration of microwave pulses generates spurious responses. While phase randomization (PR) protocol can suppress these artifacts, they rely on probabilistic averaging. This introduces an inherent statistical variance that demands excessive sequence lengths and stringent hardware capabilities for true random phase generation. Here, we propose Hadamard sensing channel (HSC), a deterministic phase-design framework based on Hadamard matrices. HSC completely eliminates the statistical variance of PR by exactly and deterministically canceling spurious signals using a finite set of orthogonal phase patterns. Simulations confirm that HSC matches the ideal suppression of PR but exhibits superior robustness against control errors. HSC offers a mathematically exact and hardware-friendly solution for reliable high-resolution nanoscale nuclear magnetic resonance.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a deterministic phase-design framework based on Hadamard matrices (HSC) to replace probabilistic phase randomization (PR) for suppressing spurious responses in dynamical decoupling sequences used in quantum sensing, eliminating statistical variance while maintaining equivalent suppression performance.
AI.motivation: Dynamical decoupling sequences are crucial for nanoscale quantum sensing, but finite-duration microwave pulses generate spurious responses. The existing phase randomization (PR) protocol suppresses these artifacts only through probabilistic averaging, which introduces inherent statistical variance, requiring excessively long sequence lengths and demanding true random phase generation from hardware.
AI.method: The authors propose Hadamard sensing channel (HSC), a deterministic phase-design framework built on Hadamard matrices. HSC uses a finite set of orthogonal phase patterns to exactly and deterministically cancel spurious signals, completely removing the statistical variance inherent in PR without relying on probabilistic averaging.
AI.result: Simulations confirm that HSC achieves the same ideal suppression performance as PR while exhibiting superior robustness against control errors, offering a hardware-friendly and mathematically exact alternative.
AI.conclusion: HSC provides a mathematically exact, deterministic, and hardware-friendly solution for reliable high-resolution nanoscale nuclear magnetic resonance, overcoming the statistical and hardware limitations of phase randomization.

title: Master equation for systems interacting with linearized gravity
summary: We investigate the open quantum dynamics of a system of two masses interacting with an environment of linearized gravitational waves. We formulate the analysis in terms of the observable proper distance between the two masses, and show that the canonical variables obtained from the standard Lagrangian, expressed in terms of the Fermi normal coordinates, are not suitable for an effective description of the system. We resolve this issue through a unitary transformation that provides a physically meaningful system--environment decomposition and derive the master equation to leading order in $G$. Its dissipative sector reproduces the classical energy loss due to gravitational-wave emission, while the noisy contributions suppress coherences between states with different mass quadrupole, or effectively, different proper separations. In the regime where the proper distance can be described by considering small quantum fluctuations around an average distance $l_0$, the dynamics reduces to a Caldeira--Leggett-type equation, with a decoherence rate dependent on the baseline length $l_0$.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes the open quantum dynamics of two masses interacting with a bath of linearized gravitational waves. The authors find that standard canonical variables in Fermi normal coordinates are unsuitable, resolve this via a unitary transformation, and derive a master equation to leading order in G. The dissipative sector matches classical gravitational-wave energy loss, while noise suppresses coherences between states with different mass quadrupole/proper separations. Near a mean separation l0, the dynamics reduces to a Caldeira-Leggett equation with a baseline-dependent decoherence rate.
AI.motivation: To obtain a physically meaningful master equation for a system of two masses coupled to a gravitational-wave environment, since the naive canonical formulation in Fermi normal coordinates fails to provide an effective description.
AI.method: The authors formulate dynamics in terms of the observable proper distance between masses, apply a unitary transformation to correct the system-environment decomposition, and derive a master equation to leading order in the gravitational constant G. In the small-fluctuation regime, they reduce it to a Caldeira-Leggett master equation.
AI.result: The master equation's dissipative sector reproduces classical gravitational-wave energy loss, and the noise term decoheres superpositions of different mass quadrupoles (equivalently different proper separations). In the small-fluctuation regime, a Caldeira-Leggett-type equation is found with a decoherence rate that scales with baseline length l0.
AI.conclusion: The proper distance is the right observable for describing two masses in a gravitational-wave environment, and the resulting open dynamics correctly encode both dissipation (classical emission) and gravitationally induced decoherence, with baseline-dependent rates.

title: Quantum Amplitude Estimation for Travel Time Estimation in Stochastic Vehicle Routing Problems
summary: Solving the Vehicle Routing Problem (VRP) in Stochastic Transportation Networks (STNs), a core task in Intelligent Transportation Systems (ITS), introduces estimation challenges for stochastic path travel times and the resulting VRP objective function. These challenges have typically been addressed through computationally expensive sampling-based techniques such as Monte Carlo simulation, whose performance depends on sample size, the sampling strategy, and the underlying travel time distributions. To address these issues, this study proposes and validates a quantum computing technique, Quantum Amplitude Estimation (QAE) for path-level travel time estimation in STNs. Without relying on sampling or prior assumptions of the travel time distribution, the proposed framework encodes all feasible travel time realizations into a quantum superposition, enabling a theoretical quadratic speed-up over Monte Carlo simulation. Four QAE variants are implemented in IBM's Qiskit framework, namely Canonical AE (CAE), Iterative AE (IAE), Maximum Likelihood AE (MLAE), and Faster AE (FAE), together with four rotation-angle scaling strategies for handling different discrete travel time distributions. Experiments on a small-scale STN show that the choice of scaling method and rotation-angle range significantly affects estimation accuracy, while the four QAE variants produce comparable estimates across all tested conditions, with IAE exhibiting the most stable overall performance. The results provide practical guidance on parameter selection for future hybrid quantum-classical optimization frameworks in ITS applications.

Four QAE variants (CAE, IAE, MLAE, FAE) with four rotation-angle scaling strategies are implemented in IBM's Qiskit framework, achieving theoretical quadratic speed-up over classical sampling. Experiments show scaling strategy significantly affects accuracy while QAE variants perform comparably, with IAE being most stable.

These methods are inefficient as their accuracy depends on sample size, sampling strategy, and underlying travel time distributions, motivating the need for a fundamentally faster and distribution-agnostic estimation approach.
AI.method: The framework encodes all feasible travel time realizations into a quantum superposition using Quantum Amplitude Estimation, eliminating the need for sampling or distributional assumptions. Four QAE variants are implemented in IBM's Qiskit: Canonical AE (CAE), Iterative AE (IAE), Maximum Likelihood AE (MLAE), and Faster AE (FAE), combined with four rotation-angle scaling strategies to handle different discrete travel time distributions.

Among the variants, Iterative AE (IAE) demonstrates the most stable overall performance, and the theoretical quadratic speed-up over Monte Carlo simulation is supported.
