title: Error-detected surgery on Iceberg codes
summary: We construct explicit error-detecting surgery gadgets---small systems of auxiliary qubits and checks---for the high-rate Iceberg codes $[[2N,2N-2,2]]$, to perform fault-detected measurements of logical Pauli products. The construction follows the perspective of surgery as the gauging of a logical operator, regarded as a symmetry of the code. We give a complete classification of logical Pauli operators under the permutation automorphism group of the Iceberg code, reducing the construction to one gadget per orbit, and we verify with circuit-level simulations that the gadgets are fault-detecting, with the expected post-selected logical error rate. The gadgets require reconfigurable long-range connectivity, available on platforms such as neutral-atom arrays, making an error-detected demonstration of Pauli-based computation a natural near-term experiment. The paper doubles as a self-contained introduction to gauging and code surgery, developed alongside a simple worked example.

AI.tldr: This paper constructs explicit error-detecting surgery gadgets for high-rate Iceberg codes [[2N,2N-2,2]], enabling fault-detected measurements of logical Pauli products. The construction uses gauging of logical operators as symmetries, classifies logical Pauli operators under the permutation automorphism group, and verifies fault-detection via circuit-level simulations. The gadgets require reconfigurable long-range connectivity, making them suitable for neutral-atom platforms.
AI.motivation: To enable fault-tolerant Pauli-based computation using high-rate Iceberg codes, error-detecting surgery gadgets are needed to perform logical Pauli measurements without full error correction, while maintaining fault-detection guarantees.
AI.method: The construction uses surgery as the gauging of a logical operator treated as a code symmetry. Logical Pauli operators are fully classified under the permutation automorphism group of the Iceberg code, reducing gadget construction to one per orbit. Circuit-level simulations verify fault-detection properties.
AI.result: Explicit error-detecting surgery gadgets are constructed and verified via circuit-level simulations to be fault-detecting with expected post-selected logical error rates. The gadgets require reconfigurable long-range connectivity available on neutral-atom arrays.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a practical path toward error-detected demonstrations of Pauli-based computation on near-term neutral-atom platforms, while also serving as a self-contained pedagogical introduction to gauging and code surgery.

title: Quantum fluctuation relations in first-detection processes
summary:
We derive two quantum fluctuation relations for systems undergoing repeated projective measurements. These fluctuation relations characterize the work that can be extracted from a quantum device when a first-detection event triggers a mechanical operation leading to positive work production. The correction to the standard quantum Jarzynski equality depends logarithmically on the mean first-detection time for the time-reversed dynamics.
  Application of Jensen's inequality leads to fundamental limits on both the total work involved in the repeated measurements and final mechanical operation, and the extracted work alone.
  The general case of a device connected to an external environment is also considered.

AI.tldr: The paper derives two quantum fluctuation relations for systems under repeated projective measurements, characterizing extractable work triggered by first-detection events. The correction to the quantum Jarzynski equality depends logarithmically on the mean first-detection time for time-reversed dynamics, and Jensen's inequality yields fundamental bounds on total and extracted work, including the case with an external environment.
AI.motivation: To generalize quantum fluctuation relations to scenarios involving repeated projective measurements, specifically characterizing work extraction when a first-detection event triggers a mechanical operation that produces positive work, and to establish fundamental thermodynamic limits in such measurement-driven processes.
AI.method: Derivation of two quantum fluctuation relations for systems under repeated projective measurements, where a first-detection event triggers a mechanical operation producing work. The relations modify the standard quantum Jarzynski equality with a correction term involving the logarithm of the mean first-detection time for time-reversed dynamics. Jensen's inequality is applied to derive thermodynamic bounds, and the formalism is extended to open systems coupled to an external environment.
AI.result: Two quantum fluctuation relations are derived for work extraction in measurement-triggered mechanical processes. The correction to the standard quantum Jarzynski equality scales logarithmically with the mean first-detection time for the time-reversed dynamics. Application of Jensen's inequality yields fundamental limits on both the total work (including repeated measurements plus the final mechanical operation) and the extracted work alone. An extension to the general case of a device coupled to an external environment is also provided.
AI.conclusion: Repeated projective measurements with first-detection triggering lead to modified quantum fluctuation relations whose deviation from the standard Jarzynski equality is governed by first-detection statistics of the time-reversed process. These relations establish fundamental thermodynamic bounds on work extraction in measurement-controlled quantum devices, both in isolated and open (environment-coupled) settings.

title: Warm-Starting MaxCut Relaxation via Low-Depth Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm
comment: 7+0 pages; 3+0 figures; v1: version accepted for the proceedings of the 2026 IEEE International Conference on Quantum Computing and Engineering (QCE); comments and suggestions are welcome!; accompanying repo: https://github.com/usra-riacs/quantum-approximate-optimization
summary: Quantum optimization has attracted growing interest as quantum hardware continues to improve, yet state-of-the-art classical solvers remain a formidable benchmark for practical utility. Rather than seeking a fully quantum replacement for classical optimization, we propose a hybrid strategy that uses quantum information to enhance leading classical heuristics. Specifically, we introduce a warm-start method based on local correlators obtained from the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA), and use this information to initialize the Burer-Monteiro (BM) rank-two relaxation. We demonstrate numerically that, compared to a random, multi-start initialization baseline (a standard strategy used for BM), this quantum-informed initialization offers a significant head start, i.e., high-quality solutions with very small number of iterations, for two problem classes -- random Erdős Rényi graphs with edge density of $10\%$ (ER-10) and fully-connected Sherrington Kirkpatrick (SK) spin glass models, at $n=500$ and $n=1000$ qubits. At the same time, given enough iterations, the random baseline often eventually catches up and slightly outperforms the warm-start strategy on average, an effect visibly stronger for $n=500$ than for $n=1000$. The results demonstrate an exploitation/exploration tradeoff of using WS to quickly arrive at very good solutions vs exploring slightly better solutions with a larger iterations budget via a standard strategy. Our results highlight how low-depth quantum circuits can provide useful structural information for classical optimization and suggest a promising route toward near-term quantum utility through quantum-assisted initialization.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a hybrid quantum-classical optimization strategy that uses QAOA-derived local correlators to warm-start the Burer-Monteiro rank-two relaxation. Numerical results on ER-10 graphs and SK spin glasses (n=500, 1000) show the quantum-informed initialization yields high-quality solutions in very few iterations compared to random multi-start baselines, though random starts can catch up with more iterations, revealing an exploitation/exploration tradeoff.
AI.motivation: Classical solvers remain strong benchmarks for optimization, and a fully quantum replacement is not yet practical. The authors seek instead to use quantum information to enhance existing classical heuristics, particularly by injecting structural information from low-depth quantum circuits into classical optimization pipelines.
AI.method: The method computes local correlators from QAOA and uses them to warm-start the Burer-Monteiro (BM) rank-two relaxation, as opposed to random multi-start initialization. The approach is tested numerically on random Erdős–Rényi graphs (10% edge density) and fully-connected Sherrington-Kirkpatrick spin glasses at n=500 and n=1000.
AI.result: The quantum-informed warm-start yields high-quality solutions with very few iterations, outperforming the random multi-start baseline as a head start. However, given enough iterations, the random baseline often catches up and slightly outperforms the warm-start on average, with this effect more pronounced at n=500 than n=1000.
AI.conclusion: The results demonstrate an exploitation/exploration tradeoff: warm-starting quickly yields excellent solutions while random multi-start can explore slightly better solutions given a larger iteration budget. Low-depth quantum circuits can provide useful structural information for classical optimization, suggesting a promising near-term route to quantum utility via quantum-assisted initialization.

title: Global vs. Product Observables in Bipartite Quantum Systems: The Sharp Bound
summary: To probe a bipartite quantum system, one may use arbitrary global operators or restrict to product operators acting separately on the two subsystems. We determine the sharp universal comparison between the resulting norms. For every $z\in M_n\otimes M_m$, we prove $\|z\|_1\leq\sqrt{2}\min\{n,m\}\|z\|_\varepsilon$, where $\|\cdot\|_1$ is the trace norm and $\|\cdot\|_\varepsilon$ is the injective tensor norm associated with the trace norms on $M_n$ and $M_m$. To prove the upper bound, we establish an $L_1$ noncommutative Khintchine inequality whose random coefficients are the entries of a Haar unitary. We also show that the coefficient $\sqrt{2}$ is sharp. As applications, we show that the same sharp constant governs the gap between bipartite correlation measured in trace norm and that measured by a correlation function, and obtain an improved universal upper bound for quantum data hiding. The upper bound has also been formalized and machine-checked in Lean.

AI.tldr: The paper establishes the sharp universal constant relating the trace norm to the injective tensor norm for bipartite quantum states, proving that ||z||_1 ≤ √2·min{n,m}·||z||_ε for all z ∈ M_n ⊗ M_m. The proof relies on a noncommutative L1 Khintchine inequality with Haar unitary coefficients, and the constant √2 is shown to be optimal.
AI.motivation: To understand the fundamental gap between probing a bipartite quantum system with arbitrary global operators versus restricting to product operators acting separately on each subsystem, one needs a sharp comparison between the corresponding norms. This has implications for quantum data hiding, entanglement detection, and correlation measurement.
AI.method: The authors prove the upper bound via a new L1 noncommutative Khintchine inequality where the random coefficients are entries of a Haar unitary matrix. Sharpness of the constant √2·min{n,m} is established, and the result is formalized and machine-checked in the Lean proof assistant.
AI.result: The paper proves that ||z||_1 ≤ √2·min{n,m}·||z||_ε for all z ∈ M_n ⊗ M_m, with the constant √2 shown to be sharp/optimal. This yields an improved universal upper bound for quantum data hiding and characterizes the gap between bipartite correlation in trace norm versus correlation function.
AI.conclusion: The sharp constant relating trace norm and injective tensor norm for bipartite systems is √2·min{n,m}, proven via a novel noncommutative Khintchine inequality. This directly translates into an improved universal bound for quantum data hiding and is additionally certified through formal proof verification in Lean.

title: Fundamental limits of parameter estimation with heralded optical non-Gaussian states generated from Gaussian resources
summary: Non-Gaussian states can exhibit large quantum Fisher information (QFI) in quantum sensing. In optical systems, however, its generation is often probabilistic via the boson-sampling type conditional operation and thus its generation rate is limited. This probabilistic generation of non-Gaussian resource should be taken into account for evaluation of the sensing performance. Then a natural question arising is whether the use of heralded probabilistic non-Gaussian states is better than that of the original deterministic Gaussian states for quantum sensing. In this paper, we answer to this question for single-parameter phase-estimation. By using photon-number conservation in passive linear optical systems, we show that heralded state preparation before parameter encoding can be mapped to a postselection problem after parameter encoding for phase estimation. This mapping allows the success probability of heralding to be included naturally in the metrological performance. We introduce an effective quantum Fisher information (EQFI), defined as the success-probability-weighted QFI of the heralded outputs, and prove that it cannot exceed the QFI of the original Gaussian inputs. The result highlights the importance of resource counting in quantum sensing toward better understanding of the resource efficient advantage of optical quantum sensing.

AI.tldr: The paper proves that for single-parameter phase estimation, the success-probability-weighted quantum Fisher information (EQFI) of probabilistically generated non-Gaussian states cannot exceed the QFI of the original deterministic Gaussian states, showing that heralded non-Gaussian preparation does not provide a metrological advantage when resource counting is considered.
AI.motivation: Non-Gaussian states can have large QFI for quantum sensing, but their generation in optical systems is often probabilistic (via boson-sampling-type conditional operations) with limited generation rates. Since probabilistic generation should be accounted for when evaluating sensing performance, a key question arises: is using heralded probabilistic non-Gaussian states better than the original deterministic Gaussian states?
AI.method: Using photon-number conservation in passive linear optical systems, the authors show that heralded state preparation before parameter encoding can be mapped to a postselection problem after parameter encoding for phase estimation. They introduce an effective quantum Fisher information (EQFI), defined as the success-probability-weighted QFI of the heralded outputs, and prove that it cannot exceed the QFI of the original Gaussian inputs.
AI.result: The EQFI of heralded probabilistic non-Gaussian states is proven to be bounded above by the QFI of the original deterministic Gaussian input states in single-parameter phase estimation.
AI.conclusion: The result highlights the importance of resource counting in quantum sensing, demonstrating that probabilistic non-Gaussian state generation does not offer a metrological advantage over deterministic Gaussian states when the success probability is properly accounted for, contributing to a better understanding of resource-efficient optical quantum sensing.

title: Exponential logical-error reduction in quantum memories via optimal syndrome-measurement timing
summary: Syndrome-measurements timing is usually treated as a fixed clock cycle of a quantum error-correcting code. For quantum memories, however, the intra-measurement interval is itself an optimizable control parameter: measuring too rarely allows idling errors to accumulate, whereas measuring too often introduces measurement-induced faults. We propose a phenomenological logical-noise model for this trade-off and analytically show that the optimal syndrome-measurements interval scales inversely proportionally with the code distance and that this produces an exponential reduction of logical-error rates in the distance relative to constant-interval schedules. Furthermore, for time-dependent idling noise, we develop an adaptive timing strategy based on the measured syndrome activity that outperforms every fixed-interval protocol, with largest gains for short but strong noise bursts. Simulations of rotated surface-code memories with matching decoding validate the phenomenological model, the distance-dependent optimum, and the adaptive-strategy improvement. Moreover, with the experimental noise parameters reported by Google in Nature 638 (2025), our model predicts reductions in logical-error rates per unit time of up to $40\%$.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes that the syndrome-measurement interval in quantum error-correcting codes is an optimizable control parameter, not a fixed clock cycle. The authors introduce a phenomenological logical-noise model showing the optimal measurement interval scales inversely with code distance, yielding exponential error-rate reduction. They also develop an adaptive timing strategy based on measured syndrome activity that outperforms all fixed-interval protocols, particularly for short, strong noise bursts. Simulations on rotated surface codes confirm the model, and using Google's experimental noise parameters, they predict up to 40% reduction in logical-error rates per unit time.
AI.motivation: Traditional quantum error correction treats the syndrome-measurement interval as fixed. However, for quantum memories there is a trade-off: frequent measurements introduce measurement-induced faults, while infrequent ones allow idling errors to accumulate. This trade-off is an unexplored control dimension that could significantly improve logical-error rates.
AI.method: The authors develop a phenomenological logical-noise model capturing the measurement-interval trade-off. They analytically derive the optimal interval scaling (inversely proportional to code distance) and propose an adaptive syndrome-activity-based timing strategy. The approach is validated via simulations of rotated surface-code memories with matching decoding, and applied to experimental noise parameters from Google's Nature publication.
AI.result: The optimal syndrome-measurement interval scales inversely with code distance and yields exponential reduction of logical-error rates relative to constant-interval schedules. The adaptive timing strategy outperforms every fixed-interval protocol, especially for short, strong noise bursts. Using Google's experimental noise parameters, the model predicts up to 40% reduction in logical-error rates per unit time.
AI.conclusion: Syndrome-measurement timing is a valuable and previously overlooked control parameter for quantum memories. Both distance-dependent optimal scheduling and adaptive syndrome-activity-based strategies offer demonstrable, analytically supported improvements in logical error rates, validated by simulations and applicable to real experimental systems.

title: Approximate Quantum Error Correction at Chiral Topological Edges
summary: Topologically ordered phases naturally realize quantum error correction through nonlocal encoding of quantum information. More recently, conformal field theories have been shown to realize approximate quantum error-correcting codes, but such constructions generally require fine tuning to criticality. Here we introduce a family of approximate quantum error-correcting codes realized by the chiral edges of two-dimensional topologically ordered phases. The proposed encoding combines the robustness of a gapped topological bulk with the flexibility of gapless edge conformal field theories. To characterize its robustness, we study coherent-information loss under local erasure. We derive an exact expression relating coherent-information loss to relative entropy, reducing the recoverability problem to universal properties of the edge theory. This leads to power-law scaling of coherent-information loss with the size of the erased region. We further show that, for geometrically local erasures near one edge, the two-dimensional chiral edge code is at least as robust as the dimensionally reduced CFT code, and is strictly more robust in several representative examples. For Abelian code subspaces, we further construct a power-law-range recovery map supported on the erased region together with a power-law-range buffer; this recovery map depends only on the code subspace, not on the unknown encoded state. We provide numerical calculations for lattice realizations of compact free boson and Ising CFT examples that support the theoretical predictions of the power-law exponents.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a family of approximate quantum error-correcting codes realized by the chiral edges of 2D topologically ordered phases, combining topological bulk robustness with edge CFT flexibility. The authors derive an exact relation between coherent-information loss and relative entropy, showing power-law scaling of error correction capability with erased region size, and construct power-law-range recovery maps for Abelian code subspaces.
AI.motivation: Topological order naturally realizes quantum error correction via nonlocal encoding, but these are typically exact codes. Approximate QEC codes from conformal field theories require fine-tuning to criticality. The authors seek to bridge these approaches by leveraging gapped topological bulks alongside gapless edge CFTs, avoiding the criticality fine-tuning problem while gaining the flexibility of CFT-based codes.
AI.method: The authors construct approximate QEC codes from chiral edge theories of 2D topologically ordered phases. They derive an exact expression connecting coherent-information loss to relative entropy, casting recoverability in terms of universal properties of the edge CFT. This yields power-law scaling of coherent-information loss with erased region size. They compare robustness against geometrically local erasures to dimensionally reduced CFT codes, and for Abelian code subspaces construct a power-law-range recovery map with a buffer that depends only on the code subspace. Numerical lattice simulations for compact free boson and Ising CFT examples corroborate the scaling predictions.
AI.result: The proposed chiral edge codes exhibit power-law scaling of coherent-information loss with erasure size, are at least as robust as dimensionally reduced CFT codes for local erasures near one edge, and are strictly more robust in several representative cases. Explicit recovery maps with power-law range are constructed for Abelian subspaces. Numerical results for compact free boson and Ising CFT lattice realizations match the predicted power-law exponents.
AI.conclusion: Two-dimensional chiral edge theories offer a promising, non-fine-tuned framework for approximate quantum error correction that integrates the protection of topological order with the flexible structure of edge CFTs. The power-law recoverability behavior and explicit recovery map constructions establish a new class of approximate codes with practical implications for quantum error correction in topological platforms.

title: Nonlinear Compton scattering in a quantized pump field
summary: We develop a fully quantized theory of nonlinear Compton scattering driven by a single-mode quantum field. Exact quantum-Volkov states retain pump depletion, back-action, and final-state correlations through displaced or squeezed-displaced Fock-state ladders. A finite Fock-state pump produces discrete photon-transfer edges and a terminal spectral cutoff. In the bright, weakly depleted regime, the exact theory reduces to a Wigner-function weighted-average of scattering probabilities evaluated at fixed complex field amplitudes, with ordinary and generalized Bessel functions describing the harmonic structure for circular and linear polarization, respectively. For squeezed coherent light, the squeezing angle controls the high-energy emission through photon-number fluctuations.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a fully quantized theory of nonlinear Compton scattering driven by a single-mode quantum field, using exact quantum-Volkov states that capture pump depletion, back-action, and correlations. It reduces to a Wigner-function weighted average in the bright, weakly depleted regime and shows that squeezed coherent light controls high-energy emission via the squeezing angle.
AI.motivation: To go beyond classical-field treatments of nonlinear Compton scattering and account for quantum-field effects such as pump depletion, back-action, and final-state correlations, which are neglected in standard approaches.
AI.method: Constructing exact quantum-Volkov states with displaced or squeezed-displaced Fock-state ladders for a single-mode pump field. The theory is analyzed in a bright, weakly depleted regime, where scattering probabilities reduce to a Wigner-function weighted-average evaluated at fixed complex field amplitudes, with ordinary Bessel functions for circular polarization and generalized Bessel functions for linear polarization.
AI.result: A finite Fock-state pump produces discrete photon-transfer edges and a terminal spectral cutoff. In the weakly depleted regime, the exact theory maps to a Wigner-function averaged scattering probability. For squeezed coherent light, the squeezing angle controls high-energy emission through photon-number fluctuations.
AI.conclusion: The fully quantized framework provides a more complete description of nonlinear Compton scattering beyond mean-field approximations, revealing quantum signatures such as discrete transfer edges, spectral cutoffs, and squeezing-dependent emission that are inaccessible to classical treatments.

title: Impact of Nonlinearities on Local Kinetic and Thermokinetic Uncertainty Relations in Bosonic Transport
summary: The precision of transport observables can be bounded by the entropy production and the activity of the transport process via kinetic and thermokinetic uncertainty relations. In linear bosonic systems, such uncertainty relations can provide tight bounds when the activity is replaced by a local activity of the measurement contact of interest---even in the strong-coupling regime. How much nonlinearities (or interactions) impact the validity and predictiveness of these local bounds and how much this impact depends on the concrete definition of activity are open questions that we address for two experimentally relevant model systems, a harmonic oscillator network and the intrinsically nonlinear spin-boson model. We thereby provide experimentally testable predictions on how nonlinearities impact or even break local kinetic and thermokinetic precision bounds.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how nonlinearities and interactions affect local kinetic and thermokinetic uncertainty relations (precision bounds) in two model systems: a harmonic oscillator network (linear) and the spin-boson model (intrinsically nonlinear). The authors examine whether replacing global activity with a local activity of the measurement contact provides tight precision bounds in the presence of nonlinearities, and how the choice of activity definition influences these bounds.
AI.motivation: Kinetic and thermokinetic uncertainty relations bound transport observables' precision via entropy production and activity. For linear bosonic systems, replacing global activity with local activity of the measurement contact yields tight bounds even in strong coupling. However, it is unclear how nonlinearities impact the validity and predictiveness of these local bounds, and how this depends on the definition of activity—open questions the paper addresses.
AI.method: The authors analyze two experimentally relevant model systems: a harmonic oscillator network (linear) and the intrinsically nonlinear spin-boson model. They systematically compare local kinetic and thermokinetic uncertainty relations using different definitions of activity to determine how nonlinearities impact or break these local precision bounds.
AI.result: The paper provides experimentally testable predictions showing how nonlinearities impact or even break local kinetic and thermokinetic precision bounds, with the effect depending sensitively on the concrete definition of activity used.
AI.conclusion: Nonlinearities can undermine the validity and predictive power of local uncertainty-relation-based precision bounds in transport processes, and the degree of this impact is strongly dependent on the chosen definition of activity.

title: Time-Reversal Selection Rules for Quantum Error Correction
summary: We apply time-reversal symmetry to quantum codes and show that it imposes parity selection rules on the physical error algebra. A time-reversal-invariant logical qubit on an odd number of spins is a Kramers doublet, forcing every even-weight Pauli to act as a scalar. Consequently, all even-weight Knill--Laflamme conditions hold automatically, so single-qubit error detection implies correction. We then reinterpret the Rains shadow enumerator through time reversal: each coefficient is a sum of error-resolved overlaps between a code and its time-reversed image.

AI.tldr: The paper applies time-reversal symmetry to quantum error-correcting codes, showing that time-reversal-invariant logical qubits on odd numbers of spins are Kramers doublets that enforce parity selection rules on Pauli errors, making even-weight Knill-Laflamme conditions automatically satisfied and connecting the Rains shadow enumerator to overlaps between a code and its time-reversed image.
AI.motivation: To uncover hidden symmetry constraints in quantum error correction by examining how time-reversal symmetry affects the structure of quantum codes and error detection/correction properties.
AI.method: The authors apply time-reversal symmetry arguments to quantum codes, showing that a time-reversal-invariant logical qubit on an odd number of spins forms a Kramers doublet, which forces all even-weight Pauli operators to act as scalars. They then reinterpret the Rains shadow enumerator in terms of error-resolved overlaps between a code and its time-reversed image.
AI.result: The parity selection rules derived from time-reversal symmetry imply that all even-weight Knill-Laflamme conditions hold automatically, so single-qubit error detection implies correction. The Rains shadow enumerator is shown to decompose as sums of error-resolved overlaps between a code and its time-reversed counterpart.
AI.conclusion: Time-reversal symmetry provides a fundamental constraint on quantum codes that simplifies error correction requirements (detection implies correction for single-qubit errors) and offers a new symmetry-based interpretation of the Rains shadow enumerator.

title: On Optimal Quantum Data Hiding and Maximal Separable Ball
summary: Quantum data hiding asks how much distinguishing power can be lost when global measurements are restricted to local measurements and classical communication. In this work, we establish sharp results and improved bounds for several natural classes of restricted measurements. For bipartite systems on $\mathbb C^n\otimes\mathbb C^m$, we prove that the optimal data-hiding ratios against separable and LOCC measurements are both $\min\{n,m\}$. This result follows from a stronger result that, for every $2\le p\le\infty$, the largest centered Schatten $p$-ball whose associated binary measurements are implementable by finite-round LOCC has radius $\min\{n,m\}^{2/p-1}$. This strengthens the classic separable-ball theorems, while also providing an explicit finite-round LOCC implementation. For Alice-first one-way LOCC with Alice's local dimension equal to $n$, we prove that the optimal ratio is $(1+o(1))n$, with the upper bound obtained from a Gaussian rank-one POVM. For local operations without communication, we improve the universal upper bound to $(π\sqrt3/4+o(1))\min\{n,m\}$.

AI.tldr: This paper establishes sharp results for quantum data hiding under restricted measurements. The optimal data-hiding ratios against separable and LOCC measurements are both min{n,m} for bipartite systems on C^n⊗C^m. For Alice-first one-way LOCC, the optimal ratio is (1+o(1))n, and for local operations without communication, an improved universal upper bound of (π√3/4+o(1))min{n,m} is proven.
AI.motivation: Quantum data hiding explores the fundamental limits of distinguishing power when global measurements are restricted to local operations and classical communication (LOCC) or other locality-constrained measurement classes. Establishing sharp bounds on data-hiding ratios is central to understanding the gap between global and local distinguishability in quantum information theory.
AI.method: The authors prove that the optimal data-hiding ratios against both separable and LOCC measurements equal min{n,m}. This follows from a stronger result: for every 2≤p≤∞, the largest centered Schatten p-ball whose associated binary measurements are implementable by finite-round LOCC has radius min{n,m}^{2/p-1}. This generalizes classic separable-ball theorems and provides explicit finite-round LOCC implementations. Additional techniques include a Gaussian rank-one POVM for the one-way LOCC upper bound and refined arguments for the no-communication case.
AI.result: Sharp data-hiding ratios: min{n,m} for both separable and LOCC measurements; (1+o(1))n for Alice-first one-way LOCC; and (π√3/4+o(1))min{n,m} for local operations without communication, improving the universal upper bound.
AI.conclusion: The work resolves the optimal data-hiding ratio for separable and LOCC measurements exactly, strengthens classical results on separable balls with explicit finite-round LOCC implementations, and provides improved bounds for one-way LOCC and no-communication local operations.

title: Dimension-Free Polylogarithmic Quantum Shadow Tomography from Sequential Pretty-Good Measurements
summary:
\textit{Shadow tomography} is a fundamental problem in quantum information theory. Given multiple copies of an unknown $d$-dimensional quantum state $ρ$ and a known collection of observables ${E_1,\ldots,E_m}$, the goal is to estimate all expectation values $\{\Tr(ρE_i)\}_{i=1}^m$ to additive accuracy $\varepsilon$ with probability at least $1-δ$.
  An elusive open question from the seminal shadow tomography work of Aaronson (STOC'18) is whether this task admits a dimension-independent sample complexity with only polylogarithmic dependence on $m$, as suggested by the best-known lower bounds. In this work, we give a quantum protocol for shadow tomography with sample complexity \[ O\left( \frac{1}{\varepsilon^2} \frac{(\log (m/δ))^4} {(\log\log (m/δ))^3} \right), \] which is polylogarithmic in the number of observables and independent of the dimension of the unknown state thereby answering Aaronson's original question while also providing an exponential improvement in the prior best dimension independent sample complexity of shadow tomography from Sinha (STOC'25).
  Our approach first reduces the general shadow-tomography problem to a finite-ensemble estimation problem via a minimax argument. We then develop an observable-independent protocol that repeatedly applies the pretty-good measurement and updates the priori distribution over the finite ensemble according to the measurement outcomes. A refined tail analysis of the resulting estimation error yields simultaneous accuracy guarantees for all observables.

AI.tldr: This paper resolves a central open question in shadow tomography by designing a quantum protocol with sample complexity O((1/ε²)·(log(m/δ))^4/(log(log(m/δ)))^3), which is polylogarithmic in the number of observables m and independent of the dimension d, thereby settling Aaronson's question and exponentially improving the prior best dimension-independent result from Sinha (STOC'25).
AI.motivation: Shadow tomography is a fundamental quantum information problem where one estimates expectation values of m known observables against an unknown d-dimensional quantum state ρ. The question of whether this can be done with dimension-independent sample complexity that is only polylogarithmic in m (as suggested by lower bounds) was left open by Aaronson in his seminal STOC'18 work. Resolving this question is crucial for understanding the fundamental limits of quantum state estimation.
AI.method: The protocol proceeds in two main steps. First, it reduces the general shadow tomography problem to a finite-ensemble estimation problem via a minimax argument. Second, it develops an observable-independent protocol that iteratively applies the pretty-good measurement, updating a prior distribution over the finite ensemble based on measurement outcomes. A refined tail analysis of the resulting estimation error provides simultaneous accuracy guarantees across all observables.

title: Bell nonlocality from twisted statistics
summary: We investigate Bell correlations for a free real quantum scalar field on the noncommutative Moyal plane. Although the free field dynamics and the one-particle sector remain unchanged, the deformation enters through twisted multiparticle statistics and its Fock-space dressing representation. The momentum-dependent twist phases are generally nonfactorizable and generate entanglement between the corresponding wave-packet modes. We show that suitable local mode measurements lead to a violation of the CHSH Bell inequality. The resulting correlations provide an operational probe of the noncommutative structure encoded in the multiparticle sector of the quantum field.
